Alessandro Nesta.why: Nesta was a centre-back who made defending look smooth and calm. He rarely needed to dive in, because he read where the ball was going before the attacker did. When he did tackle, he slid in cleanly and came away with the ball. He was also comfortable on the ball, so he could start attacks straight after winning it. Kids can copy his patience: stay on your feet, watch the ball, and only tackle when you are sure.

learn.text: Nesta waited for the right moment to win the ball. Practise jockeying: stand side-on with your knees bent, a short distance from the attacker. Keep your eyes on the ball, not on their tricks. Step in only when they push the ball too far ahead.

facts.text: Nesta joined Lazio's youth teams in 1985 and later became club captain. Lazio won the UEFA Cup Winners' Cup in the 1998-99 season with him in the side.
He was named Serie A Defender of the Year four years in a row, from 2000 to 2003, and was part of the Italy team that won the 2006 World Cup.

Alfredo Di Stéfano.why: Di Stéfano was a forward who seemed to be everywhere on the pitch. He would drop deep to win the ball, carry it forward, play a pass and then arrive in the box to finish the move himself. His energy set the pace for the great Real Madrid side of the 1950s, and team-mates followed his lead. Kids can learn from his work rate: a striker can help the team in every part of the field, not just near goal.

learn.text: Di Stéfano never stopped working when his team lost the ball. Practise the quick sprint back: as soon as the ball is lost, turn and race to get between the attacker and your own goal, then slow down and face them.

facts.text: His nickname was 'Saeta Rubia', which means 'The Blond Arrow'. The name was coined by an Argentine journalist called Roberto Neuberger.
Di Stéfano won the Ballon d'Or in 1957 and again in 1959. Years before moving to Europe, he helped Argentina win the 1947 Copa América.

Andrea Pirlo.why: Pirlo played just in front of his defenders, in a role Italians call the regista, or director. He was not the fastest runner or the hardest tackler. Instead he looked up early, found space and picked passes that opened up whole teams. He kept the ball moving at his own pace, so the game seemed to slow down around him. Young players can copy his habit of checking around them before the ball arrives.

learn.text: Pirlo struck long passes with a smooth, relaxed swing. Practise with a partner standing far away: plant your standing foot beside the ball, strike through the middle of it and follow through towards your target.

facts.text: At the 2006 World Cup, Pirlo was voted the third-best player of the tournament and won the Bronze Ball. His corner set up Italy's equaliser in the final.
With AC Milan he won the Champions League in 2003 and 2007. After moving to Juventus in 2011, he won four Serie A titles in a row.

Andrés Iniesta.why: Iniesta was a midfielder who could slip past defenders without ever seeming to hurry. He used tiny touches, sudden changes of pace and his body to shield the ball. When opponents pressed him, he stayed calm, kept possession and found a team-mate. He also popped up with goals in the biggest matches of all. Kids can copy the way he kept the ball close while looking up for the next pass.

learn.text: Iniesta kept the ball glued to his feet in tight spaces. Practise dribbling with small touches, using both the inside and outside of your foot. When a defender comes close, put your body between them and the ball.

facts.text: Iniesta was named man of the match in the 2010 World Cup final, a game that gave Spain its first-ever World Cup title.
He was chosen as Player of the Tournament at Euro 2012 and won the UEFA Best Player in Europe award in the same year.

Arjen Robben.why: Robben was a right winger who loved to drift inside onto his stronger left foot. Defenders knew what was coming, yet his speed and timing still beat them. He would carry the ball along the edge of the box, then curl a shot towards the far corner. His bursts of pace over a few metres made him very hard to catch. Kids can learn how practising one move again and again can turn it into a real weapon.

learn.text: Robben's favourite move was to cut inside and curl the ball. Practise dribbling along a line, then take a sharp touch inside onto your stronger foot. Look up at the far post and bend the ball there with the inside of your foot.

facts.text: Robben won the Premier League twice with Chelsea, in 2005 and 2006, and then won La Liga in his first season with Real Madrid.
In 2010, after his first season at Bayern Munich, he was named Footballer of the Year in Germany. He went on to win eight Bundesliga titles there.

Ashley Cole.why: Ashley Cole was a left-back who made life very hard for fast wingers. He stayed close to his opponent, showed them down the line and used quick feet to block crosses. If he got caught upfield, he sprinted back to cover. He could also overlap and join attacks. His concentration lasted the whole match. Kids can learn that a full-back's first job is to stop the winger getting a clean run at goal.

learn.text: Cole was famous for chasing back fast when a winger got past him. Practise this: when an attacker breaks away, sprint on a curved path to get between them and your goal. Then turn to face them and slow them down.

facts.text: Cole came through Arsenal's youth teams and won seven FA Cups, three with Arsenal and four with Chelsea. That is more than any other player in history.
He won the Champions League with Chelsea in 2012, scoring in the penalty shootout of the final against Bayern Munich. He also played 107 times for England.

Bobby Moore.why: Bobby Moore was a centre-back who was not quick, so he learned to stay one step ahead in his mind. He read the game, stepped in to cut out passes and timed his tackles perfectly. Once he had the ball, he calmly passed it to a team-mate instead of kicking it away. As captain he stayed composed in big moments. Kids can copy the way he watched the play and moved early instead of chasing.

learn.text: Moore read the game by looking around before the ball came near him. Practise turning your head to check over each shoulder every few seconds, so you always know where the attackers are and can step in to cut out a pass.

facts.text: In 1966 Moore became the first footballer to win the BBC Sports Personality of the Year award. He went on to play 108 times for England.
A bronze statue of Bobby Moore stands at the entrance to Wembley Stadium. He led England as captain 90 times, equalling Billy Wright's record.

Cafu.why: Cafu was a right-back who seemed never to run out of energy. He guarded his side of the pitch, then charged forward on overlapping runs to support the winger and send in crosses. Moments later he would be racing back to defend again. He kept playing at the top level for many years thanks to his fitness. Kids can learn from his stamina and his eagerness to join the attack whenever there was space.

learn.text: Cafu loved to overlap. Practise with a team-mate: pass the ball to them, then sprint past on the outside. They play the ball back into your path so you can run onto it at full speed.

facts.text: Cafu captained Brazil to the 2002 World Cup and lifted the trophy. He had already won the 1994 World Cup, coming on in that final.
In 1994 he was named South American Footballer of the Year. In Italy he won Serie A with Roma in 2001 and with AC Milan in 2004.

Carles Puyol.why: Puyol was a centre-back who threw everything into every challenge. He was not the tallest defender, but he made up for it with courage, energy and a refusal to give up on any ball. He blocked shots, chased down quick forwards and organised the players around him. As Barcelona's captain he led by example in every match. Kids can learn from his effort: never stop working until the danger is gone.

learn.text: Puyol never gave attackers a moment's peace. Practise closing down quickly but under control: sprint towards the attacker, then take small steps as you get close. Stay low and keep watching the ball until you can win it.

facts.text: Puyol first played football as a goalkeeper for his hometown club in La Pobla de Segur. Later he played as a forward before finding his place in defence.
He captained Barcelona from 2004 until 2014 and played 593 competitive matches for the club, winning six La Liga titles and three Champions Leagues.

Carlos Alberto.why: Carlos Alberto was a right-back who loved to join the attack. In an era when many defenders stayed back, he raced forward down the flank and arrived in the box with perfect timing. He could strike the ball hard and true. As captain he also guided his team-mates and kept them organised. Kids can learn from his bravery: a defender can create chances too, as long as someone covers the space behind.

learn.text: Carlos Alberto timed his runs from deep so he arrived just as the ball did. Practise running onto a pass that a team-mate rolls into your path, then strike it first time, keeping your head down and your body over the ball.

facts.text: His nickname was 'o Capitão do Tri', the captain of Brazil's third World Cup title. In 2004 Pelé named him in the FIFA 100 list of the greatest living players.
Later in his career he joined the New York Cosmos, where he teamed up again with Pelé and helped the club win the NASL title in 1977 and 1978.

Cristiano Ronaldo.why: Cristiano Ronaldo started out as a skilful winger who loved stepovers and quick dribbles. Over the years he turned himself into one of the deadliest finishers the game has seen. He worked hard on his fitness, his shooting with both feet and his runs into the box. He is famous for his dedication to training. Kids can learn that skill grows with practice, and that a player can keep improving year after year.

learn.text: Ronaldo can score with either foot, which makes him hard to stop. Practise shooting with your weaker foot as often as your strong one. Lock your ankle, point your toe down and strike through the middle of the ball.

facts.text: In 2008, while playing for Manchester United, Ronaldo won his first Ballon d'Or at the age of 23. He became the third Portuguese winner after Eusébio and Luís Figo.
He led Portugal to their first major international trophy at Euro 2016, and he also helped them win the UEFA Nations League in 2019 and 2025.

Dani Alves.why: Dani Alves was a right-back who played almost like an extra winger. He bombed forward, swapped quick passes with team-mates and whipped in crosses. His link-up play with Messi on Barcelona's right side became famous. Even with all that attacking, he still sprinted back to defend. He brought joy and energy to every game. Kids can copy his love of short, sharp passing moves that cut through a defence.

learn.text: Alves often played a quick one-two to get past defenders. Practise passing the ball against a wall or to a friend, then moving straight away to receive the return in space. Keep your touches short and sharp.

facts.text: Before joining Barcelona, Alves won the UEFA Cup twice with Sevilla, in 2006 and 2007. At Barcelona he went on to win the Champions League three times.
At the 2019 Copa América, Brazil won the title and Alves was named the tournament's best player. Two years later he won Olympic gold with Brazil at Tokyo 2020.

Daniel Passarella.why: Passarella was a centre-back and a natural leader. He was not especially tall, yet he won battles against bigger forwards through timing and determination. He also loved to push forward and was a real goal threat for a defender. Team-mates trusted him to organise the back line and keep everyone focused, which is why he became known as the great captain. Kids can learn that defenders can lead, talk and score too.

learn.text: Passarella led his team by talking. In small games, practise calling out to your team-mates: tell them 'man on', 'time' or 'turn' so they know what is around them before the ball arrives.

facts.text: Eight years after lifting the trophy in 1978, Passarella was again in Argentina's squad when they won the 1986 World Cup, giving him two winner's medals.
As a coach, he later led Argentina at the 1998 World Cup and then became the first foreigner to manage Uruguay's national team.

Dino Zoff.why: Dino Zoff was a goalkeeper who made saving shots look simple. Instead of flashy dives, he relied on smart positioning, so the ball often came straight to him. He stayed calm under pressure and gave his defenders confidence. His focus and fitness let him play at the top level for a very long time. Kids can learn that a goalkeeper who stands in the right place does not need to make as many big saves.

learn.text: Zoff was known for always being in the right spot. Practise taking a step or two off your line and standing on an imaginary line between the ball and the middle of your goal. Shuffle your feet as the ball moves.

facts.text: Between 1972 and 1974, Zoff went 1,142 minutes without conceding a goal for Italy, the longest run of its kind in international football.
Zoff won the European Championship with Italy in 1968. Many years later, as Italy's coach, he guided the team all the way to the final of Euro 2000.

Edwin van der Sar.why: Van der Sar was a tall goalkeeper who was also brilliant with his feet. He was happy to receive back-passes and start attacks with calm, accurate passes and kicks. He stayed cool in big matches and rarely made mistakes. His steady voice organised the defence in front of him. Kids can learn that goalkeepers are part of the team's passing game, not just shot-stoppers waiting on the line.

learn.text: Van der Sar often started attacks with a pass instead of a big kick. Practise receiving a back-pass, taking a touch out of your feet, then looking up and passing along the ground to a free team-mate.

facts.text: In the 2008-09 season he set a Premier League record by going 1,311 minutes without conceding a league goal for Manchester United.
He saved Nicolas Anelka's kick to win the 2008 Champions League final shootout. He played his last match in the 2011 final, aged 40, and then retired.

Eusébio.why: Eusébio was a forward with explosive speed and a thunderous right-footed shot. He could burst past defenders from a standing start, then strike the ball with huge power from distance. Benfica fans called him the King, and he scored goals at every level, from Mozambique to Portugal to the World Cup. Kids can learn from his acceleration: the first few steps after beating a player are what create space for a shot.

learn.text: Eusébio exploded away from defenders with his first few steps. Practise turning with the ball, then pushing it a little further ahead and sprinting onto it. Use short, quick strides at the start, like a sprinter leaving the blocks.

facts.text: Eusébio was the first player ever to win the European Golden Shoe as Europe's top league scorer, in 1968, and he won it again in 1973.
He scored twice in the 1962 European Cup final as Benfica beat Real Madrid 5-3. A statue of him stands outside Benfica's Estádio da Luz.

Fabio Cannavaro.why: Cannavaro was a centre-back who was shorter than most of the strikers he faced. He made up for it with quick reactions and brilliant timing. He read where passes were going and darted in front of attackers to steal the ball before they could control it. He was also a calm, encouraging captain who never seemed rattled. Kids can learn that reading the game matters far more than being big.

learn.text: Cannavaro loved to step in front of an attacker and steal the pass. Practise as a defender in the middle of a passing circle: watch the passer's hips and eyes, guess where the ball is going and move early to cut it out.

facts.text: As a boy, Cannavaro was a ball boy at his local club Napoli, where he would watch his heroes Diego Maradona and Ciro Ferrara play.
In 2006 he was named FIFA World Player of the Year, the only defender ever to win that award. Earlier, he won the UEFA Cup with Parma in 1999.

Franck Ribéry.why: Ribéry was a left winger full of tricks and energy. He kept the ball very close as he twisted past defenders, then looked up to cross or set up a team-mate. He did not stop when his team lost the ball; he chased back to help his full-back. His partnership with Arjen Robben on the opposite wing made Bayern very hard to defend against. Kids can copy his mix of close control and hard work.

learn.text: Ribéry dribbled with lots of tiny touches to stay in control at speed. Practise weaving through a line of cones using the inside and outside of both feet. Keep your head up between touches so you can spot a pass.

facts.text: In 2008 he was named Footballer of the Year in Germany after his first season at Bayern Munich. Two years earlier, he had played for France in the 2006 World Cup final.
In August 2013 he won the UEFA Best Player in Europe award, and he finished third in the voting for the 2013 Ballon d'Or.

Franco Baresi.why: Baresi was a sweeper and centre-back who led one of the most famous defences ever. He constantly talked to his team-mates, moving the whole back line up and down together. He read danger early and stepped in to win the ball cleanly. Once he had it, he often carried it forward himself. He was not big, but he was brave and always focused. Kids can learn how a defender's voice can organise a whole team.

learn.text: Baresi kept talking to the defenders beside him. Practise defending as a pair and use short, clear words such as 'step', 'drop' and 'I've got him'. One player presses the ball while the partner covers and calls.

facts.text: When Baresi retired in 1997, AC Milan retired his number 6 shirt. Two years later, in 1999, he was voted Milan's Player of the Century.
He was back in the team just in time to play in the 1994 World Cup final, where he gave a commanding display at the heart of Italy's defence.

Frank Rijkaard.why: Rijkaard was a tall, strong player who could do almost every job on the pitch. He protected his defence from midfield, won the ball with clean tackles and then passed it simply and quickly to start attacks. He could also play at centre-back when needed. His calm style made the team-mates around him better. Kids can learn from his simple, smart play: win the ball, then give it to a free team-mate straight away.

learn.text: After winning the ball, Rijkaard usually played a quick, simple pass to keep his team moving. Practise keep-away in small groups: when your team wins the ball, look up at once and find the nearest free player with a short pass.

facts.text: Rijkaard scored the only goal of the 1990 European Cup final as AC Milan beat Benfica 1-0. In 1995 he won the Champions League again, this time with Ajax against Milan.
As a coach, he later guided Barcelona to Champions League glory in 2006, when they beat Arsenal 2-1 in the final.

Franz Beckenbauer.why: Beckenbauer played as a sweeper behind his defenders, but he did not just stay back. When his team won the ball, he would glide forward into midfield, play neat passes and even join attacks. He made difficult moves look easy and always seemed to have time on the ball. His calm style changed how people thought defenders could play. Kids can learn that defenders can be creative and help build attacks from the back.

learn.text: Beckenbauer often brought the ball out of defence himself. Practise receiving a pass from your goalkeeper, then dribbling forward into open space when nobody presses you. Look up and pass to a midfielder once a defender comes close.

facts.text: In 1990 Beckenbauer coached West Germany to the World Cup, beating Argentina 1-0 in the final. That made him one of the very few people to win it as both player and manager.
He won three European Cups in a row with Bayern Munich, from 1974 to 1976, and also won the 1972 European Championship with West Germany.

Gabriel Batistuta.why: Batistuta was a centre-forward famous for hitting the ball incredibly hard. He was strong enough to hold off defenders, then turn and shoot in one movement. He could score from close range or from far outside the box, and goalkeepers often had no time to react. He worked hard for the team even when matches were tough. Kids can learn how a clean strike with the laces can beat a goalkeeper.

learn.text: Batistuta struck the ball with fierce power. Practise shooting with your laces: point your toes down, keep your knee over the ball and land on your kicking foot. Aim low and hard into the corners of the goal.

facts.text: Batistuta was the first player to score hat-tricks at two different World Cups, against Greece in 1994 and against Jamaica in 1998.
In 1996, Fiorentina fans put up a life-size bronze statue of him. He also won the Copa América twice with Argentina, in 1991 and 1993.

Garrincha.why: Garrincha was a right winger who loved to take on defenders one against one. He would slow down, wait, then shoot off in a new direction before the defender could react. Fans adored his playful style and the joy he brought to the game. He made dribbling look like fun rather than hard work. Kids can copy his fearless attitude: be brave, try your moves and enjoy every touch of the ball.

learn.text: Garrincha beat defenders with sudden changes of speed and direction. Practise dribbling slowly towards a defender, then fake one way and explode the other. A quick drop of the shoulder before you go helps sell the fake.

facts.text: At the 1962 World Cup in Chile, Garrincha was the star of Brazil's win while Pelé missed most of the tournament, finishing as joint top scorer with four goals.
His nickname 'Garrincha' is the name of a small bird, the wren, and was given to him by his sister. Brazil never lost a match when he and Pelé played together.

Gary Neville.why: Gary Neville was a right-back who could be trusted every single week. He was disciplined, kept his position and rarely let wingers past him easily. When the chance came, he overlapped to support the attack and deliver crosses. He came through Manchester United's youth team alongside a group of friends and stayed at the club for his whole career. Kids can learn that hard work and concentration can take a player a very long way.

learn.text: Neville and Beckham linked up down the right with quick passes. Practise in a triangle of three: pass, then move to a new spot so the ball can come back to you. Keep it moving with one or two touches.

facts.text: Neville won eight Premier League titles with Manchester United and was made club captain in 2005, after Roy Keane left the club.
He won the Champions League with United in 1999 and 2008, played 85 times for England, and in 2025 was inducted into the Premier League Hall of Fame.

George Best.why: George Best was a winger with amazing balance. He could ride tackles, glide past defender after defender and keep the ball under control at top speed. He used both feet and was brave enough to dribble into crowded areas. Above all, his dribbles usually ended with a goal or a chance for a team-mate. Kids can copy his balance: stay light on your feet, keep your body low and keep the ball close when defenders come in.

learn.text: Best kept his balance even when defenders bumped into him. Practise dribbling at a partner with your knees bent and your arms out a little for balance. Use both feet and try to get past them to score in a small goal.

facts.text: Best was spotted in Belfast at the age of 15 by Manchester United scout Bob Bishop. He went on to help United win league titles in 1965 and 1967.
On 7 February 1970 he scored six goals in one FA Cup match as United beat Northampton Town 8-2. Belfast City Airport was later renamed in his honour.

Gerd Müller.why: Gerd Müller was a striker who lived in the penalty area. He was short and stocky, with a low centre of gravity that let him turn sharply in tight spaces. He always seemed to be in the right spot when the ball dropped near goal. He did not need many touches; often one was enough to score. Kids can learn his poacher's habit: stay alert near goal and react first to every loose ball.

learn.text: Müller reacted faster than defenders when the ball came loose. Practise following every shot towards goal, whether it is yours or a team-mate's. If the goalkeeper spills it, be first to the rebound and tap it in.

facts.text: At the 1970 World Cup, Müller scored ten goals to win the Golden Boot, and later that year he won the Ballon d'Or.
He scored the winning goal in the 1974 World Cup final against the Netherlands. In 1971-72 he netted 40 Bundesliga goals, a record that stood until 2021.

Gianluigi Buffon.why: Buffon was a goalkeeper with superb positioning and a calm, confident presence. He commanded his area, organised his defenders loudly and made hard saves look routine. He was always balanced and ready, so he could react fast to anything. He kept his passion for the game over a remarkably long career. Kids can learn from his focus: a goalkeeper must be ready for every shot, even after a quiet spell with nothing to do.

learn.text: Buffon was always balanced when a shot came. Practise the set position: feet shoulder-width apart, knees bent, weight on the front of your feet and hands out in front. Get set just before the striker shoots.

facts.text: Buffon made his Serie A debut for Parma at just 17, in November 1995. A few years later he helped Parma win the UEFA Cup in 1999.
At the 2006 World Cup he won the Yashin Award as the best goalkeeper. He is also the only goalkeeper to win UEFA's Club Footballer of the Year award, for 2003.

Gordon Banks.why: Gordon Banks was a goalkeeper known for lightning reactions and smart positioning. He worked out angles carefully, so he was rarely caught out of place. He had safe hands and made catching look easy, which gave his defenders great confidence. Even in the biggest games he stayed calm. Kids can learn from his reliability: do the simple things well, like catching cleanly and getting your body behind the ball.

learn.text: Banks was known for safe, sure hands. Practise catching high shots with your hands in a W shape, thumbs almost touching behind the ball. For low balls, scoop them up into your chest like a basket.

facts.text: Banks was named FIFA Goalkeeper of the Year six times in a row, from 1966 to 1971, and he won 73 caps for England.
He won the League Cup twice, with Leicester City in 1964 and with Stoke City in 1972, and was the Football Writers' Footballer of the Year in 1972.

Iker Casillas.why: Casillas was a goalkeeper with incredibly fast reflexes. He was quick off the ground and brilliant at spreading himself to block shots in one-on-ones. He stayed calm when the pressure was highest, which made him a trusted captain for club and country. His best saves often came at the most important moments. Kids can learn from his quick feet and sharp focus: stay on your toes, stay low and react to the ball.

learn.text: Casillas was always on his toes, ready to spring. Practise small, quick steps across your goal, then stop in a balanced position each time a friend shows you the ball. React and dive as soon as it is struck.

facts.text: In 2000, just four days after his 19th birthday, Casillas became the youngest goalkeeper to play in and win a Champions League final.
At the 2010 World Cup he won the Golden Glove as the best goalkeeper, and he was named the IFFHS World's Best Goalkeeper a record five times.

Javier Zanetti.why: Zanetti could play right-back, left-back or in midfield, and he did each job with the same energy. He ran up and down the pitch all game, carried the ball forward with strong, determined dribbles and still tracked back to defend. He looked after his fitness so well that he played at the top level for many seasons. Kids can learn that being reliable and willing to play anywhere makes you very valuable to a team.

learn.text: Zanetti often powered forward with the ball from defence. Practise dribbling through small gates spread around an area, keeping the ball close and your head up so you can pick out the next gate.

facts.text: His nickname was 'El Tractor', earned for his stamina and tireless running. He also scored in the 1998 UEFA Cup final, which Inter won.
Zanetti played 858 matches for Inter, more than anyone in the club's history. In 2015 the club retired his number 4 shirt in his honour.

Lev Yashin.why: Lev Yashin changed what people expected from a goalkeeper. Instead of staying on his line, he came out to deal with crosses and through balls, and he shouted orders to his defenders. He dressed in dark kit, and his long reach made strikers feel he had eight arms. He was also famous for saving penalties. Kids can learn that a goalkeeper can be a leader who helps the defence, not just someone who stops shots.

learn.text: Yashin came off his line to close down attackers. Practise starting on your line, then taking quick steps out towards a striker who is dribbling at you. Stay big and low, and stop moving just before they shoot.

facts.text: Yashin won Olympic gold at the 1956 Games in Melbourne and the 1960 European Nations' Cup with the Soviet Union, keeping goal both times.
As a young man he also played ice hockey for Dynamo and won the Soviet ice hockey cup in 1953. FIFA named its World Cup goalkeeper award after him in 1994.

Lionel Messi.why: Messi is a left-footed attacker who keeps the ball incredibly close while running at full speed. His low centre of gravity lets him change direction in a flash, leaving defenders off balance. He also sees passes others miss and finishes with clever, calm shots rather than wild ones. He makes the hardest skills look simple. Kids can copy his tiny, quick touches: the ball should never be more than a step away when you dribble.

learn.text: Messi touches the ball on almost every stride when he dribbles. Practise dribbling around an area, stopping and starting when a friend calls out. Use tiny touches with the inside and outside of your foot so you can stop in an instant.

facts.text: Messi joined Barcelona's youth academy, La Masia, at 13 and made his competitive first-team debut in 2004, aged 17. In 2008 he won Olympic gold with Argentina.
In October 2023 he received a record eighth Ballon d'Or. His wins came in 2009, 2010, 2011, 2012, 2015, 2019, 2021 and 2023.

Lothar Matthäus.why: Matthäus could do almost every job in midfield. He tackled hard, then burst forward with the ball at his feet and hit shots from far out. He never seemed to get tired, so he helped his team at both ends of the pitch. Later in his career he even dropped back to play as a sweeper behind the defence. Young players can copy his energy and his bravery to carry the ball into open grass when nobody closes him down.

learn.text: When there is space in front of you, push the ball a few steps ahead and run onto it at speed. Keep your head up as you go. Once you reach shooting range, take one settling touch and strike it low and hard.

facts.text: Matthäus played at five FIFA World Cups in a row, from 1982 to 1998. He was the first outfield player ever to appear at five tournaments.
In 1990 he won the Ballon d'Or. Nine years later, aged 38, he was voted German Footballer of the Year for a second time.

Luís Figo.why: Figo was a right winger who loved to take on his full-back. He used quick feints and changes of pace to make a yard of room, then whipped the ball into the box. Defenders found it hard to guess which way he would go. He could also cut inside and pass or shoot. Figo shows young players that a winger's job is not finished after beating a defender: the final ball matters most.

learn.text: Before you cross, take a quick look into the box to see where your teammates are running. Lock your ankle, lean slightly back and strike through the side of the ball so it curls away from the goalkeeper.

facts.text: As a teenager, Figo won the 1991 FIFA World Youth Championship with Portugal, playing alongside Rui Costa and João Pinto in a famous 'golden generation'.
Figo was named FIFA World Player of the Year in 2001. He also won the Champions League with Real Madrid in 2002 and four Serie A titles with Inter.

Manuel Neuer.why: Neuer changed how many people think about goalkeeping. He stands far off his line so he can race out and clear danger before an attacker gets a shot away. He is also calm with the ball at his feet, so his team can pass back to him and start attacks from the back. A young keeper can learn from Neuer that good feet, quick decisions and brave positioning are part of the job, not just diving.

learn.text: Practise passing with both feet like an outfield player. When a defender passes back to you, open your body, take a soft first touch out of your feet, then pass firmly along the ground to a free teammate.

facts.text: Neuer won the Golden Glove for the best goalkeeper at the 2014 World Cup in Brazil. Later that year he finished third in the Ballon d'Or voting.
Born in Gelsenkirchen, he came through every youth team at his hometown club Schalke and won the German Cup with them in 2011.

Marco van Basten.why: Van Basten was a tall, graceful centre-forward who made hard skills look simple. He could control a dropping ball in one touch and then strike it before defenders reacted. He scored with either foot, from tight angles and from long range. His balance meant he rarely fell over when shooting. Kids can learn from his clean technique: watch the ball closely, stay relaxed and keep your body over the ball when you strike.

learn.text: When a high ball drops towards you, get under it early. Let it land on your thigh or chest and relax so it drops softly at your feet. Then you have time to set yourself and shoot.

facts.text: On his Ajax debut in April 1982, the teenage Van Basten came on as a substitute for Johan Cruyff and scored in a 5-0 win.
In November 1992 he became the first player to score four goals in a single Champions League match, for Milan against IFK Göteborg.

Michel Platini.why: Platini was a playmaker who scored like a striker. He spotted gaps in the defence, played clever passes, and then sneaked into the box at just the right moment to finish. He was also brilliant at free kicks, bending the ball over the wall. Platini teaches young players that a midfielder can be a goal threat by timing runs well and staying calm when the chance arrives.

learn.text: Don't rush into the box too early. Wait just outside while your striker holds the ball, then jog in as they lay it back. Arriving late means no defender is marking you, so you can shoot first time.

facts.text: Platini scored nine goals at Euro 1984, including two hat-tricks, against Belgium and Yugoslavia, as captain of the winning France side.
He was Serie A's top scorer for three seasons in a row, from 1982-83 to 1984-85, and won the European Cup with Juventus in 1985.

Nílton Santos.why: Nílton Santos was a left-back at a time when full-backs were expected to stay at home and only defend. He was so comfortable on the ball that he would win it, carry it up the pitch and join the attack. People called him The Encyclopedia because he seemed to understand everything about the game. Today's attacking full-backs follow the path he opened. Kids can copy his calm control and his courage to step forward.

learn.text: After you win the ball in defence, look up. If the space ahead is empty, carry it forward with small touches instead of kicking it away. Keep the ball close so you can pass when an opponent finally comes to stop you.

facts.text: At the 1958 World Cup he scored against Austria after running forward from left-back, a famous early example of a full-back joining the attack.
Botafogo, the only professional club he ever played for, named its home ground the Estádio Olímpico Nilton Santos in his honour.

Oliver Kahn.why: Kahn was a goalkeeper who never gave up on any shot. He had lightning reflexes and threw his body in the way of the ball again and again. He also shouted orders to his defenders all game, keeping them organised and alert. The press called him Der Titan. Young keepers can learn from his focus: stay switched on for the whole match, because one big save can win it.

learn.text: Just before the shooter strikes, stop moving and get set. Feet shoulder-width apart, knees a little bent, weight on the front of your feet and hands ready in front. A balanced, still keeper can push off fast to either side.

facts.text: In the 2001 Champions League final against Valencia, Kahn saved three penalties in the shoot-out to win Bayern Munich the trophy.
Kahn won the UEFA Best European Goalkeeper award four years running, from 1999 to 2002, and lifted eight Bundesliga titles with Bayern.

Paolo Maldini.why: Maldini was a defender who rarely needed to slide in. He read the game so well that he was usually in the right spot before the danger arrived. When he did tackle, it was clean and perfectly timed. He played at left-back and centre-back and stayed calm with the ball. Maldini shows young defenders that patience and good positioning beat wild lunges almost every time.

learn.text: Facing a dribbler, stay on your feet and stand side-on, a short step away. Shuffle backwards and watch the ball, not their tricks. Only poke the ball away when they push it too far from their foot.

facts.text: Maldini made his Serie A debut for Milan in January 1985, aged just 16, coming on as a substitute in a match against Udinese.
He won the European Cup or Champions League five times. When he retired in 2009, Milan retired his famous number 3 shirt.

Paul Scholes.why: Scholes was a central midfielder who made the ball do the work. He could fizz a short pass into a teammate's feet or drop a long ball onto someone's chest from far across the pitch. Even top players said he was the hardest opponent to get the ball off. He also crept forward late and struck powerful shots from outside the box. Scholes shows kids that passing well is a skill worth practising every day.

learn.text: Before the ball reaches you, glance around so you already know your next pass. Use the inside of your foot, point your standing foot at your target and give the ball enough pace that it arrives quickly but is easy to control.

facts.text: Scholes scored both goals on his Manchester United debut, a 2-1 League Cup win at Port Vale in September 1994.
In the 2008 Champions League semi-final he hit a shot from about 25 yards to beat Barcelona 1-0 and send United to the final, which they won.

Pelé.why: Pelé could do everything a forward needs. He was fast, strong and balanced, he shot well with both feet, and he could see a pass that others missed. He kept calm in the biggest games and loved to score. Growing up, he practised with whatever he could find to kick. Pelé shows young players that joy, hard work and using both feet can take you a very long way.

learn.text: Give your weaker foot just as many shots as your stronger one. Start close to the goal, aim for the corners and strike with your laces. When both feet feel natural, a defender can never force you onto one side.

facts.text: Pelé was only 17 when Brazil won the 1958 World Cup, making him the youngest player ever to win the tournament. He scored twice in the final.
As a boy he often played with a grapefruit or a sock stuffed with newspaper. In 1999 the International Olympic Committee named him Athlete of the Century.

Peter Schmeichel.why: Schmeichel was a huge goalkeeper who made himself look even bigger. When a striker ran through, he rushed out, spread his arms and legs wide, and blocked the shot with any part of his body. He also yelled instructions to keep his defence tidy. Once he caught the ball, he could hurl it a long way to start a fast counter-attack. Young keepers can copy his bravery and his quick thinking after a save.

learn.text: When an attacker is coming towards goal, take a few quick steps off your line towards the ball. Standing closer makes the goal look smaller to the shooter. Stay on your feet as long as you can, then spread wide to block.

facts.text: In October 2001, playing for Aston Villa against Everton, Schmeichel became the first goalkeeper ever to score a Premier League goal.
He was voted the IFFHS World's Best Goalkeeper in 1992 and 1993, and won five Premier League titles with Manchester United.

Philipp Lahm.why: Lahm was not tall or powerful, but he was nearly always in the right place. He defended by thinking ahead, stepping in to steal the ball or blocking a pass before it happened. He played on the right, on the left and in central midfield, and he looked comfortable in every role. Lahm proves to small players that brains, balance and clean technique matter more than size.

learn.text: When your teammate goes to press the player with the ball, don't charge in too. Drop a few steps behind and to the side of them. If the attacker gets past, you are ready to step in and stop them.

facts.text: Lahm scored the first goal of the 2006 World Cup, curling a shot into the top corner after six minutes of Germany's opening match against Costa Rica.
He joined Bayern Munich's youth teams at the age of 11 and captained the club to the Champions League in 2013 with a win over Borussia Dortmund at Wembley.

Rio Ferdinand.why: Ferdinand was a centre-back who looked relaxed even under pressure. He read danger early, so he could step in front of a striker and take the ball cleanly. If an attacker did get away, his long stride and speed let him recover. He was also happy to bring the ball out from the back and pass into midfield. Ferdinand shows kids that defenders can be calm, clever footballers, not just blockers.

learn.text: If an attacker gets past you, don't chase their heels. Sprint back on a line between them and your own goal. Once you are back in front, slow down, turn side-on and make them go wide.

facts.text: Ferdinand first played for England in November 1997 against Cameroon, aged 19. At that time he was the youngest defender ever to play for England.
He came through West Ham's youth system, won the 2008 FIFA Club World Cup with Manchester United and was named England captain in 2010.

Roberto Carlos.why: Roberto Carlos was a left-back who played as if he were a winger. He was short, strong and very quick, and he charged up the touchline to join attacks all match long. Then he sprinted back to defend. His left foot struck the ball with huge power, especially from free kicks. Kids can copy his energy and his habit of making a run forward after every pass.

learn.text: Pass the ball to a teammate, then sprint straight past the defender. Your friend passes it back into the space ahead of you. Don't stand and watch after you pass; the run you make next is what breaks a defence open.

facts.text: In June 1997, at the Tournoi de France, he scored against France with a free kick from about 40 yards that bent around the wall in a huge curve.
He finished runner-up for FIFA World Player of the Year in 1997 and for the Ballon d'Or in 2002, and won 125 caps for Brazil.

Romário.why: Romário was a small striker who was nearly impossible to mark in the penalty box. He would stand still, then dart away from his defender in a flash. He needed only a tiny bit of space and one touch to get the ball under control. Then he finished quickly, often with a sneaky toe-poke before the keeper was ready. Kids can learn from his sharp movement and calm finishing.

learn.text: When you are through on goal, don't blast it. Glance at the keeper and see which side has more space. Keep your body relaxed, then pass the ball into the corner, low and early, before the keeper gets set.

facts.text: Romário was top scorer at the 1988 Olympic Games in Seoul with seven goals, where Brazil won silver. A year later he scored the only goal of the Copa América final.
He was named FIFA World Player of the Year in 1994, the year Brazil won the World Cup, after finishing as runner-up in 1993.

Ronaldinho.why: Ronaldinho played football with a smile. He had a huge bag of tricks, from step-overs to the elastico, and he used them to wrong-foot defenders and open up space. He could look one way and pass the other. He also bent free kicks and long shots into the net. Ronaldinho reminds every young player that football should be fun, and that creativity comes from hours of playing with the ball.

learn.text: Pick one trick, like a step-over or a body feint, and practise it slowly. When it feels smooth, do it faster while moving towards a cone. A good trick sells a fake first, then you burst away the other way.

facts.text: In November 2005 Ronaldinho scored twice as Barcelona beat Real Madrid 3-0 at the Bernabéu, and the home fans gave him a standing ovation.
He was part of the first Brazil team to win the FIFA U-17 World Championship, in 1997. In 2013 he led Atlético Mineiro to their first Copa Libertadores.

Ronaldo Nazário.why: Ronaldo was a striker who could beat defenders while running at full speed. He mixed rapid step-overs with sudden bursts, so players backing away never knew when he would go. When he reached the goalkeeper, he often dropped a shoulder, rounded him and rolled the ball in. His power and balance made it look easy. Kids can copy his bravery in running at defenders and his calm touch when face to face with the keeper.

learn.text: When you run at a defender, slow down just before you reach them. Do a quick fake, like a step-over or a dropped shoulder. The moment they lean the wrong way, explode past on the other side with a big push of the ball.

facts.text: Ronaldo was in Brazil's squad at the 1994 World Cup aged 17 but did not play. Four years later he won the Golden Ball as the best player of the 1998 World Cup.
He won the Ballon d'Or in 1997 aged 21, which made him its youngest winner, and was named FIFA World Player of the Year three times.

Roy Keane.why: Keane was a central midfielder who covered every blade of grass. He hunted the ball, won it back with strong, well-timed challenges and then usually played a quick, simple pass to keep his team moving. He demanded high standards from himself and from everyone around him. Young players can learn from his work rate and from the way he kept things simple once he had the ball.

learn.text: When you defend in a pair, one player presses the ball while the other blocks the easiest pass. Work together and stay close. When you win the ball, look for a short, safe pass straight away instead of dribbling.

facts.text: Keane joined Nottingham Forest from Irish club Cobh Ramblers in 1990 and made his league debut that season under manager Brian Clough.
He won seven Premier League titles and four FA Cups with Manchester United, and was inducted into the Premier League Hall of Fame in 2021.

Ruud van Nistelrooy.why: Van Nistelrooy lived in the penalty area. He worked out where the ball was likely to land before anyone else, then got there first. He kept moving to lose his marker, held the ball up strongly with his back to goal and finished with a clean first touch. Many of his goals came from very close range. Kids can learn that strikers score lots by being in the right place, not only by hitting spectacular shots.

learn.text: Every time a teammate shoots, sprint towards the goal. Keepers often spill the ball or it bounces off the post. If you are already running in, you can tap in the rebound while defenders are still watching.

facts.text: In 2003 he scored in 10 Premier League games in a row for Manchester United, a league record until Jamie Vardy managed 11 in 2015.
Van Nistelrooy was top scorer in three Champions League seasons and won Spain's Pichichi award with Real Madrid in 2006-07.

Ryan Giggs.why: Giggs was a left winger who glided past defenders. He kept the ball close to his left foot and used tiny touches and swerves of his body to change direction at speed. Later he moved into central midfield, where his passing and experience helped his team. He looked after his fitness so well that he kept playing at the top for many years. Kids can copy his close control and his balance when running fast.

learn.text: Dribble at speed using small, soft touches with the outside and inside of your foot. Keep the ball close enough that you could stop at any moment. Stay low and lean slightly forward so you keep your balance when you swerve.

facts.text: Giggs scored a famous solo goal against Arsenal in the 1999 FA Cup semi-final replay, a run often listed among the best goals of his career.
He is the only player to score in each of the first 21 Premier League seasons, and was the first to win PFA Young Player of the Year twice in a row.

Sepp Maier.why: Maier was a goalkeeper with quick hands and springy legs, which is why fans called him a cat. He was famous for being reliable: week after week he caught crosses, held shots and kept his team calm. He also loved to make people laugh, and he wore huge gloves at a time when most keepers used small ones. Young keepers can learn from his safe handling and his steady, cheerful attitude.

learn.text: For a shot at chest height or above, make a W shape with your thumbs and fingers behind the ball. For a low shot, scoop it into your chest like a basket. Always try to hold the ball rather than push it away.

facts.text: Maier played 442 Bundesliga matches in a row for Bayern Munich between 1966 and 1979, a German record that no other player has matched.
He won three European Cups in a row with Bayern, from 1974 to 1976, and later coached goalkeepers for Germany and Bayern, mentoring Oliver Kahn.

Sergio Ramos.why: Ramos was a defender who never gave up, even in the last seconds of a big game. He started as a right-back and became one of the best centre-backs of his era. He was strong in duels, quick to cover danger and confident bringing the ball out to start attacks. Kids can learn from his fighting spirit and his belief that a match is never over until the final whistle.

learn.text: When you win the ball in defence, don't just kick it long. Lift your head and check for a free teammate in midfield. If the pass is on, play it firmly along the ground; if not, pass sideways to keep the ball.

facts.text: Ramos won the 2010 World Cup and the European Championships of 2008 and 2012 with Spain, and earned a national-record 180 caps.
He came through Sevilla's youth system and made his first-team debut in February 2004. He later scored in two different Champions League finals, in 2014 and 2016.

Stanley Matthews.why: Matthews was a right winger who loved to face up to his full-back and tease him. He would lean one way, drop his shoulder, then whip the ball the other way and race down the line. After beating his man, he crossed for his strikers to score. He trained hard every day and looked after his body, which helped him play for so long. Kids can copy his patient dribbling and his clever feints.

learn.text: When a defender blocks your way, slow down and lean your body to one side as if you are going there. When they shift their weight, push the ball the other way with the outside of your foot and sprint.

facts.text: Matthews won the very first Football Writers' Association Footballer of the Year award in April 1948, while he was playing for Blackpool.
In 1965 he became the only footballer ever knighted while still an active professional player. He earned 54 England caps between 1934 and 1957.

Steven Gerrard.why: Gerrard was a midfielder who could change a game on his own. He made tackles, sprayed long passes and charged forward from deep to arrive in the box. When the ball sat up for him outside the area, he hit it with fierce power. As captain, he lifted his teammates when things were going badly. Kids can learn from his never-say-die attitude and his clean, powerful shooting technique.

learn.text: To hit a powerful shot, place your standing foot beside the ball, pointing at the goal. Keep your head down and your knee over the ball. Strike through the middle with your laces and land on your kicking foot.

facts.text: In the 2006 FA Cup final against West Ham he scored a stoppage-time equaliser from around 35 yards. Liverpool then won on penalties, and fans called it the 'Gerrard final'.
Gerrard joined Liverpool's academy in 1989, aged nine. In 2006 his fellow professionals voted him PFA Players' Player of the Year.

Thierry Henry.why: Henry was a striker who often drifted out to the left wing, then ran at defenders with long, smooth strides. When he cut inside, he loved to side-foot the ball into the far corner, placing it rather than smashing it. He also set up lots of goals for teammates. His manager, Arsène Wenger, turned him from a winger into a centre-forward. Kids can learn from his calm finishing and his clever use of space.

learn.text: Instead of blasting every shot, try passing the ball into the net. Open your body and use the inside of your foot to curl it towards the far post. Aim just inside the post, where the keeper can't reach.

facts.text: Henry won the 1998 World Cup and Euro 2000 with France. He also won the Premier League Golden Boot a record four times.
Back at Arsenal on a short loan in January 2012, he came off the bench against Leeds United in the FA Cup and scored the only goal.

Xavi Hernández.why: Xavi was a small central midfielder who almost never lost the ball. Before it reached him, he turned his head again and again to see where opponents and teammates were. That meant he already knew his next pass. He kept the ball moving with short, accurate passes and set the speed of his team's play. Xavi teaches kids that looking around before you receive is one of the most important habits in football.

learn.text: While the ball is travelling towards you, quickly turn your head to look over each shoulder. Spot where the space is and who is closing in. Then, when the ball arrives, you already know whether to turn or pass back.

facts.text: Xavi joined Barcelona's La Masia academy at the age of 11. His 767 appearances for the club stood as a record until Lionel Messi passed it in 2021.
He was named Player of the Tournament at Euro 2008, when Spain beat Germany in the final. Nine years earlier he had won the FIFA World Youth Championship.

Zinedine Zidane.why: Zidane was a playmaker who made the ball look glued to his feet. He used every part of his foot, including the sole, to shield it, spin away from defenders and glide into space. He stayed calm when surrounded and found passes that split the defence. He grew up playing with friends on a plaza in Marseille. Kids can learn from his soft touch and his calm head under pressure.

learn.text: When the ball comes to you, cushion it by letting your foot move back slightly as it arrives. Try using the sole too, rolling the ball to the side. A soft, controlled first touch buys you time to look up.

facts.text: Zidane was named FIFA World Player of the Year three times, in 1998, 2000 and 2003. UEFA also named him Player of the Tournament at Euro 2000.
As a coach, he led Real Madrid to three Champions League titles in a row, becoming the first coach ever to achieve this.

Petr Čech.why: Čech was a very tall goalkeeper who made saving look simple. Instead of diving wildly, he moved his feet quickly so he was already in the right place when the shot came. He stayed calm, organised his defence and rarely made mistakes. In the 2012 Champions League final he saved a penalty in extra time and two more in the shoot-out. Young keepers can learn that good positioning means fewer difficult saves.

learn.text: As the ball moves around the box, take small side steps so you always stay in line with it. Don't cross your feet. When the attacker gets ready to shoot, stop, get set and stay balanced.

facts.text: In the 2004-05 season Čech went 1,025 minutes without conceding a Premier League goal, which was a league record at the time.
He is the most capped player in Czech Republic history, with 124 caps, and was named Czech Footballer of the Year more times than anyone else.

David Seaman.why: Seaman was a calm, tall goalkeeper whom fans trusted completely. He rarely flapped at crosses or dropped easy shots, so his defenders felt safe in front of him. He positioned himself well, which meant many saves looked simple. When needed, he could also throw himself across the goal at full stretch. Young keepers can learn from his steady hands and his habit of staying composed, even when the pressure was high.

learn.text: Get your body behind the ball whenever you can, so if it slips through your hands your chest or legs stop it. Watch the ball right into your gloves, then hug it tight before you move.

facts.text: At Euro 96 Seaman saved a penalty from Scotland's Gary McAllister in a group game, then stopped a spot kick in the shoot-out against Spain. UEFA named him in its Team of the Tournament.
In the 2003 FA Cup semi-final against Sheffield United, aged 39, he dived back across goal to keep out an effort from Paul Peschisolido and protect a 1-0 lead.

Fabien Barthez.why: Barthez was a goalkeeper with lightning-quick reactions. He liked to come off his line early to snuff out danger, and he was comfortable playing the ball with his feet when it was passed back to him. His confidence spread to the defenders around him. Barthez shows young keepers that being brave, alert and good with the ball can make the whole team better.

learn.text: After you make a catch, look up straight away. If a teammate is free, roll or throw the ball quickly to their feet before the other team can get back. A fast, accurate throw can start an attack in seconds.

facts.text: Barthez won the 1993 Champions League with Marseille. At the time he was the youngest goalkeeper ever to win the competition.
He shares the record for most World Cup clean sheets, ten, with England's Peter Shilton. He was named best goalkeeper of the 1998 World Cup.

Jorge Campos.why: Campos was a short goalkeeper who made up for his size with speed and spring. He sprinted out of his goal to sweep up through balls and leapt high to tip shots away. He was also so skilful that his club sometimes played him up front. His bright, self-designed shirts made him easy to spot. Campos shows kids that a keeper can be daring, athletic and comfortable with the ball.

learn.text: Stand a few steps off your line so you can reach balls played over your defence. Watch the passer. If the ball is going behind your defenders, decide quickly and go: a late, half-hearted rush is the most dangerous choice.

facts.text: Early in his career at Pumas, Campos asked to play as a striker because the club already had a first-choice keeper. He scored 14 goals in a season.
He won 129 caps for Mexico, including the CONCACAF Gold Cup in 1993 and 1996 and the 1999 FIFA Confederations Cup.

Marcelo.why: Marcelo was a left-back with the touch of a playmaker. He started playing futsal as a boy, a small game full of quick touches in tight spaces. He loved to overlap, dribble past opponents and set up goals with clever passes or flicks. He always seemed to enjoy himself on the pitch. Kids can copy his close control and the joy he brought to every game.

learn.text: Practise rolling the ball with the sole of your foot: forwards, backwards and sideways. Then try quick toe taps, switching feet. These small touches help you keep the ball close when an opponent is right next to you.

facts.text: Marcelo scored on his Brazil debut in September 2006, a 2-0 win over Wales. He went on to win the 2013 FIFA Confederations Cup with Brazil.
He won Olympic bronze in 2008 and silver in 2012, and was named in the FIFPro World XI six times.

Lilian Thuram.why: Thuram was a defender who could do two jobs. He played centre-back or right-back, and sometimes even in midfield. He was physically strong and very hard to dribble past, and he had a knack for taking the ball cleanly off attackers. When a winger tried to race past him, he stayed calm, stayed close and waited for the right moment. Copy his patience: a good defender does not dive in, but picks the moment to win the ball.

learn.text: When an attacker runs at you, stay on your toes about one big step away. Turn your body sideways so you can run either way. Keep your eyes on the ball, not their feet, and only reach in when the ball rolls too far from them.

facts.text: In the 1998-99 season Thuram won both the UEFA Cup and the Coppa Italia with Parma, two trophies in one year in Italy.
Thuram was born in Guadeloupe in the French West Indies, and two years after the World Cup he helped France win Euro 2000 as well.

Patrice Evra.why: Evra did not start out as a defender. As a young player he was a striker, then a winger, and only later became a left-back at Nice. That attacking past helped him love running forward down the left side, then sprinting all the way back to defend. He became captain of Manchester United and of France. His lesson for kids is simple: keep trying new positions, because the one you end up loving might surprise you.

learn.text: When your team loses the ball, don't stop and watch. Turn and sprint back on a curved path so you end up between the attacker and your own goal. Once you are there, slow down, get low and get ready to defend.

facts.text: Evra played the full match for Monaco in the 2004 Champions League final, where the French club reached the last game of Europe's top competition.
With Manchester United he won the 2008 FIFA Club World Cup, beating Ecuador's LDU Quito in the final, and he later won two Serie A titles with Juventus.

Giacinto Facchetti.why: Facchetti changed what people thought a full-back could do. He began as a forward and midfielder, so when Inter made him a left-back he kept his attacking instincts. Tall and hard-working, he would gallop forward from defence, join the attack and pop up in the box to score. Back then, defenders mostly stayed at home, so he was a pioneer. Kids can copy his bravery: if the space ahead is open, a defender is allowed to run into it.

learn.text: As a defender, pass the ball to a team-mate just ahead of you, then sprint forward straight away into the space down the side. Shout or point so they know you are running. Your team-mate can then pass it back into your path.

facts.text: Facchetti scored 59 goals in Serie A, which made him the highest-scoring defender in the whole history of the Italian league.
He won the European Cup with Inter in 1964 and 1965, and the club later retired the number 3 shirt in his honour.

John Terry.why: Terry was a centre-back who led by example. Pundits praised his positioning and anticipation, which meant he was often in the right place before the danger even arrived. He was strong, determined and never gave up on a ball. As captain he talked constantly, organising the players around him. Kids can learn from how he read the game: watch where the ball is going next, not just where it is now, and move early to stop the attack.

learn.text: Defending with a friend works best when one of you presses the player with the ball and the other stays a few steps behind, at an angle. If the attacker beats the first defender, the covering defender is already there to stop them.

facts.text: Terry made his Chelsea first-team debut on 28 October 1998, coming on late as a substitute in a League Cup game against Aston Villa.
He was voted PFA Players' Player of the Year for 2004-05 and was named UEFA Club Defender of the Year in 2005, 2008 and 2009.

Jamie Carragher.why: Carragher was a striker as a boy and an attacking midfielder when he first arrived at Anfield. He then became a full-back, and later one of Liverpool's most trusted centre-backs. People admired his organisation, positioning and tactical awareness, and he was famous for last-ditch recovery tackles when an attacker looked certain to score. He was always talking, telling team-mates where to stand. His lesson for kids: use your voice, because a defence that talks is much harder to beat.

learn.text: Talk to your team-mates while you defend. Use short, loud words like 'Step up!', 'Drop!' or 'I've got him!' so everyone knows their job. Practise calling out who is marking who every time the ball moves to a new player.

facts.text: In the 2000-01 season Carragher helped Liverpool win a cup treble: the FA Cup, the League Cup and the UEFA Cup.
His 737 games for Liverpool are the second-most in the club's long history, behind only Ian Callaghan, and the most by any player in the Premier League era.

Nemanja Vidić.why: Vidić was a tough, determined centre-back who hated giving strikers any room. Team-mates praised his aggressive style, and experts admired his excellent positioning and decision-making. He quickly became a leader wherever he went: he captained Red Star Belgrade as a young player and later Manchester United. Kids can copy his commitment. He stuck tight to the striker, made strong but fair challenges and always seemed to know the right moment to step in.

learn.text: Stay close to the striker you are marking, about an arm's length away, so they never feel free. When the ball comes to them, step in quickly before they can turn. Keep your body between them and the goal at all times.

facts.text: Vidić was named Premier League Player of the Season in 2008-09 and 2010-11, and he is the only defender to win that award twice.
He was appointed Manchester United club captain in 2010 and held the armband for four years, after also winning the 2008 FIFA Club World Cup with the club.

Gerard Piqué.why: Piqué grew up in Barcelona's famous La Masia academy, then moved to England with Manchester United before returning home. He mixed strength and tackling with lovely passing, and experts praised how well he read the game. Instead of booting the ball away, he liked to pass it calmly to a team-mate and start the attack from the back. When his team was losing late on, he would sometimes even push up front to help.

learn.text: When you win the ball in defence, take one touch to get it under control and look up before you pass. Find the closest free team-mate and give them a firm, flat pass along the ground. Keep it simple and keep the ball.

facts.text: Piqué returned to Barcelona in 2008 and won the treble in his very first season back, 2008-09, and then a second treble in 2014-15.
He won nine La Liga titles with Barcelona across his career there, the first in 2008-09 and the last of them in the 2022-23 season.

Thiago Silva.why: Thiago Silva became known as one of the most graceful defenders of his time. Even the great Brazilian striker Ronaldo compared his elegance to Franz Beckenbauer, the German legend. He rarely rushed. He tracked attackers carefully, stepped in at the right moment to intercept a pass, and then kept the ball calmly. He captained Brazil and won trophies in Italy, France and England. His lesson is that defending well is about timing and patience, not panic.

learn.text: Great defenders know where everyone is. While the ball is far away, take quick looks over each shoulder to spot the attackers near you. Then, when a pass comes, you already know where to move to step in front and steal it.

facts.text: Thiago Silva captained Brazil to victory at the 2013 FIFA Confederations Cup, played on home soil, and was also in the squad that won the 2019 Copa America.
At the Olympic Games he won two medals with Brazil: a bronze medal at Beijing in 2008 and then a silver medal in London in 2012.

Giorgio Chiellini.why: Chiellini tried many positions as a boy. He started in central midfield, moved out to the wing, and then found a home at left-back before becoming one of the best centre-backs in the world. Experts admired his awareness, his sense of position and the way he read the game. He covered lots of ground and loved putting pressure on attackers early. Kids can copy his never-give-up spirit and his habit of guessing what an opponent will do next.

learn.text: Watch the attacker's hips and the ball, not their tricks. If they push the ball too far ahead, that is your moment to step in. If not, keep backing off slowly while staying between them and the goal, so they never get a clear shot.

facts.text: Chiellini was part of the Italy team that won the bronze medal in the football tournament at the 2004 Summer Olympics in Athens.
On 5 November 2022 he lifted the MLS Cup with Los Angeles FC after they beat Philadelphia Union in a penalty shoot-out.

David Beckham.why: Beckham was known for his range of passing, his crossing and his set pieces. Playing on the right of midfield, he could whip the ball into the box from almost anywhere, and goalkeepers feared his free kicks. Coaches also praised how hard he worked for the team. He scored many goals straight from free kicks. What Beckham teaches: a skill like bending the ball only grows when you practise it again and again.

learn.text: To bend a cross, strike the ball with the inside of your foot, just off-centre. Wrap your foot around the ball and follow through across your body. Aim for the space between the goalkeeper and the defenders, not straight at anyone.

facts.text: On 17 August 1996, against Wimbledon, Beckham scored from the halfway line with a shot that floated over the goalkeeper and into the net.
He is the only English player to win a league title in four different countries: England, Spain, the United States and France. With LA Galaxy he won the MLS Cup in 2011 and 2012.

Frank Lampard.why: Lampard was a central midfielder who scored like a striker. His trademark was the late run: he waited outside the box while defenders watched the forwards, then burst into space at the last second to meet the ball. He also loved a shot from distance. He was famously reliable too, turning up week after week. Kids can learn that you don't need to be the fastest player to score goals; you need smart timing and the courage to shoot.

learn.text: Wait a moment before you run into the box. Wait just outside while the striker holds the ball. As they lay it back to you, run onto it and shoot first time, keeping your head over the ball and your laces pointed down.

facts.text: Lampard scored 177 Premier League goals, the most ever by a midfielder in the competition. He was also named FWA Footballer of the Year in 2005.
He played 164 Premier League games in a row before the run ended in December 2005, and he captained Chelsea in the 2012 Champions League final.

Kaká.why: Kaká was an attacking midfielder with explosive pace. When he picked up the ball near halfway, he could accelerate past defenders as if they were standing still, gliding through gaps before playing a defence-splitting pass or scoring himself. One writer said his runs had the power of a freight train. Kids can learn from how he used space: get your head up, spot the gap, then push the ball into it and sprint.

learn.text: When you see open grass ahead, push the ball a few steps in front of you with your laces and chase it at full speed. Big touches when there is space, small touches when a defender is close. Finish with a calm shot.

facts.text: Kaká was voted 2007 FIFA World Player of the Year with 1,047 votes, finishing ahead of both Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo.
He scored in the final as Milan beat Boca Juniors 4-2 to win the 2007 FIFA Club World Cup, and he received the Golden Ball as the tournament's best player.

Luka Modrić.why: Modrić was once called too light for top football, yet he became one of the best midfielders ever. Harry Redknapp, his coach at Tottenham, said the little man could take the ball in the tightest areas and beat a defender with a trick or a pass. He worked hard with and without the ball, and trained like a demon. He is famous for curling passes with the outside of his foot. His story shows kids that size does not decide how good you can be.

learn.text: In a crowded space, keep the ball very close with small touches and keep your head up. Use the outside of your foot to slip the ball away from a player coming towards you. Always know where the next free gap is.

facts.text: Modrić won the Golden Ball as the best player of the 2018 World Cup, and four years later he led Croatia to third place at the 2022 World Cup.
When he won the 2018 Ballon d'Or he became the first player other than Lionel Messi or Cristiano Ronaldo to win the award since 2007.

Toni Kroos.why: Kroos was a right-footed midfielder famous for the long range and accuracy of his passing. Experts also praised his vision. Calm and unhurried, he could find team-mates near or far, and he created goals from corners and free kicks with his deliveries. Kids can copy his calmness: a simple, well-weighted pass that keeps the ball is often better than a risky one.

learn.text: Before the ball reaches you, glance around so you already know where your next pass is going. Open your body to face the pitch. Then pass with the inside of your foot, firmly and along the ground, straight to your team-mate's feet.

facts.text: As a teenager Kroos won the Golden Ball as the best player at the 2007 FIFA U-17 World Cup, where he also scored five goals.
He won four La Liga titles with Real Madrid and was the first German to win the European Cup with two different clubs.

Patrick Vieira.why: Vieira was a tall, powerful central midfielder who did a bit of everything. He was a strong tackler, pressed hard and won the ball back to start attacks. Then, instead of passing sideways, he often made surging runs forward from midfield, carrying the ball past opponents. He mixed pace, strength and stamina. Kids can copy the way he defended and attacked in the same move: win it, look up, then drive forward.

learn.text: After you win the ball back, don't stand still. Take your first touch forward into space, away from the player you just beat. Then lift your head, carry the ball a few steps and find a team-mate further up the pitch.

facts.text: Vieira was born in Dakar, Senegal. Two years after the 1998 World Cup, he also won Euro 2000 with France.
He scored the winning penalty in the 2005 FA Cup final shoot-out for Arsenal, then won four Serie A titles in a row with Inter Milan.

Bobby Charlton.why: Charlton played as an attacking midfielder, winger or centre-forward, and he was famous for a powerful shot with either foot. He also passed accurately, which let him control the pace of games. Just as admired was the way he behaved. He was cautioned only twice in his whole career and never argued with referees or opponents. Kids can learn two things from him: practise shooting with both feet, and always play fair.

learn.text: Take turns: one shot with your right foot, the next with your left. Plant your standing foot beside the ball, lock your ankle and hit through the middle with your laces. Then defenders can't guess which way you will shoot.

facts.text: Charlton won the Ballon d'Or in 1966, and he scored twice in the 1968 European Cup final as Manchester United beat Benfica 4-1 after extra time.
His 49 goals made him England's record scorer for decades, until Wayne Rooney passed him in 2015. He was knighted in 1994.

Diego Maradona.why: Maradona was mostly left-footed, and he had strong legs and a low centre of gravity that gave him amazing balance. That let him twist and turn through crowds of defenders with the ball glued to his foot. He also had wonderful vision, close control and creativity, so he could spot a pass nobody else saw. Kids can copy the way he kept the ball tight while running, then lifted his eyes to find the best option.

learn.text: Bend your knees and stay low, like a coiled spring. Take tiny touches with the outside and inside of your favourite foot so the ball never gets more than a step away. The lower you are, the quicker you can change direction.

facts.text: Maradona won the Golden Ball as the best player of the 1986 World Cup by a unanimous vote, and in 1989 he helped Napoli win the UEFA Cup against Stuttgart.
In 2000 he was named one of the two winners of FIFA's Player of the Century award, alongside Pelé. Napoli later renamed its stadium the Stadio Diego Armando Maradona.

Johan Cruyff.why: Cruyff was a thinker on the pitch. In the 'Total Football' style he played for Ajax and the Netherlands, players swapped positions freely, and he could pop up as a winger, a striker or a midfielder. He was quick and clever, and he understood space better than almost anyone. His famous turn fooled defenders into thinking he would cross. Kids can learn his biggest idea: use your brain, and fake one way before you go the other.

learn.text: Pretend you are about to pass or cross. Instead of kicking, drag the ball behind your standing leg with the inside of your foot. Turn your body and accelerate away in the new direction while the defender is still guessing.

facts.text: Cruyff won the Golden Ball as the best player of the 1974 World Cup, even though the Netherlands lost the final.
In his first season at Barcelona, 1973-74, he helped the club win La Liga for the first time in 14 years. As Barcelona's coach he later won four league titles and a European Cup.

Rivaldo.why: Rivaldo was a left-footed attacker with a magic touch. He could dribble past defenders, bend free kicks around walls and strike powerfully from distance. He was also famous for bicycle kicks, which most players would never dare to try in a match. His playing style mixed skill with bravery. Kids can learn from his left foot: he practised so much that he could make the ball curve, dip or fly exactly where he wanted.

learn.text: To curl a shot into the far corner, strike the ball with the inside of your foot and wrap it around the side of the ball. Lean slightly over it to keep it low. Aim just inside the post, away from the goalkeeper.

facts.text: Rivaldo was named FIFA World Player of the Year in 1999, and he won consecutive La Liga titles with Barcelona in 1998 and 1999.
In 2001 he completed a hat-trick against Valencia with an 89th-minute bicycle kick, sending Barcelona into the Champions League. He later won the 2003 Champions League with Milan.

Hristo Stoichkov.why: Stoichkov was a left-footed forward with explosive pace. He loved dribbling at speed, racing down the left before cutting in to unleash a powerful shot. He was also dangerous from free kicks. With Johan Cruyff's Barcelona 'Dream Team', he gave the attack energy and a fierce will to win. Kids can learn from his directness: when a gap opens, attack it quickly and be brave enough to shoot.

learn.text: When you face a defender out wide, run at them fast. Push the ball past their side with a big touch, then sprint after it. Once you are inside, take a quick look at the goal and shoot before they can recover.

facts.text: In 1990 Stoichkov scored 38 league goals in 30 matches for CSKA Sofia and received the European Golden Shoe as Europe's top scorer.
He helped Barcelona win La Liga four times in a row, from 1991 to 1994, and led Bulgaria to fourth place at the 1994 World Cup.

Pavel Nedvěd.why: Nedvěd was a wide midfielder with explosive pace and huge energy. He made deep runs from midfield, crossed with his left foot and cut inside to shoot with his right. He was known for his tackling and work rate too, so he helped his team defend as well as attack. Italian fans loved his passion so much they nicknamed him 'Furia Ceca', the Czech Fury. Kids can copy his effort: run hard both ways, every game.

learn.text: Practise cutting inside. Dribble down the side, then use the inside of your outside foot to push the ball across towards the middle. Take one more touch to set it, and shoot with the other foot before a defender can block.

facts.text: Nedvěd scored the decisive goal as Lazio beat Mallorca 2-1 in the 1999 Cup Winners' Cup final, and he helped Lazio win Serie A in 1999-2000.
He played for the Czech Republic team that surprised many people by reaching the Euro 1996 final, where they lost 2-1 to Germany.
