Eden Hazard.why: Hazard was an attacker known for his dribbling, creativity and vision. He was short and sturdy, which made him hard to knock off the ball, and he could change direction in a flash. Defenders often had to foul him to stop him. He did not only dribble; he looked for team-mates and set up goals as well. Kids can learn from his calm with the ball: shield it, wait for the defender to commit, then glide away.

learn.text: When a defender gets close, put your body between them and the ball. Keep the ball on the foot furthest from them. Wait for them to lean in, then drop your shoulder and slip away the other way with a quick touch.

facts.text: At Lille, Hazard won Ligue 1 in 2010-11 and was the youngest player ever named Ligue 1 Player of the Year, winning it again the next season.
He won the PFA Players' Player of the Year award in 2015, scored twice in Chelsea's 2019 Europa League final win, and received the Silver Ball at the 2018 World Cup.

Wayne Rooney.why: Rooney spent most of his career as a forward but could also play in midfield, so coaches could use him almost anywhere. He burst onto the scene as a teenager and played with energy, never stopping his chasing and pressing. He could score with power, but he also loved to pass and set up team-mates. Kids can copy his attitude: work hard for the team, and you will get chances to shine.

learn.text: After you shoot, don't stand and watch. Keep running towards goal in case the keeper spills the ball or it bounces back off the post. Be ready to tap in the rebound before the defenders react.

facts.text: On 19 October 2002, aged 16, Rooney scored a last-minute winner for Everton against Arsenal, ending Arsenal's 30-match unbeaten run.
He scored a hat-trick on his Manchester United debut, a 6-2 Champions League win over Fenerbahçe in September 2004, and was named PFA Players' Player of the Year in 2010.

Alan Shearer.why: Shearer was a classic number 9. He was strong, could hold the ball up with his back to goal and bring team-mates into play, and he had a fierce shot. He was also an expert penalty taker, one of the most successful in Premier League history. Early in his career he was praised for clever runs into space. Kids can learn from his confidence in front of goal: pick your spot early and strike it firmly.

learn.text: As a striker, practise holding the ball with your back to goal. Keep your body strong and arms wide, take a touch to control it, then pass it back to a team-mate running forward. Spin away and get ready for the return ball.

facts.text: At 17 years and 240 days, Shearer scored a hat-trick against Arsenal for Southampton, becoming the youngest player to score a top-division hat-trick.
He won the Premier League with Blackburn in 1994-95, was top scorer at Euro 96, and became Newcastle's all-time top scorer with 206 goals.

Didier Drogba.why: Drogba was a powerful target man. Defenders struggled with his physical strength, his pace and his powerful, accurate shooting. He was brilliant at holding the ball with his back to goal, which gave team-mates time to join the attack. In the biggest games he seemed to grow even stronger. Kids can learn from how he used his body: stay strong, protect the ball, and let your team catch up before you pass or turn.

learn.text: When the ball is played up to you, lean back gently into the defender so you can feel where they are. Control the ball on the foot furthest from them. If they stand too tight, roll around the other side and turn towards goal.

facts.text: Drogba was named African Footballer of the Year in 2006 and 2009, and he won the Premier League Golden Boot in 2006-07 and 2009-10.
He was the first African player to score 100 Premier League goals. In the 2012 Champions League final he scored a late equaliser and then the winning penalty.

Samuel Eto'o.why: Eto'o was a fast, strong and energetic forward. He was extremely quick in his prime and brilliant at timing his runs, so he was often one step ahead of defenders when the pass arrived. He finished accurately with both his feet and his head, and he worked very hard for the team, even chasing back to help defend. Kids can learn from his clever running: move just before the pass, not after it.

learn.text: Timing is everything. Stand level with the last defender, and as your team-mate gets ready to pass, sprint into the space behind. If you go too early you are offside; too late and the gap closes. Practise starting your run on their backswing.

facts.text: Eto'o won Olympic gold with Cameroon at the 2000 Sydney Games, and he won the Africa Cup of Nations in 2000 and 2002.
With 18 goals, he is the all-time leading scorer in Africa Cup of Nations history. He also scored in both the 2006 and 2009 Champions League finals.

Zlatan Ibrahimović.why: Ibrahimović was a tall, strong striker who moved like a much smaller player. He was known for acrobatic strikes and volleys, lovely ball control and great technique, as well as his physical power. He would try things other players would not even imagine, like flicks, back-heels and overhead kicks. Kids can learn that a big player can still have soft, skilful feet; practise touch and control as much as strength.

learn.text: When a high ball drops towards you, watch it all the way down. Let it land on your thigh or chest and relax that part of your body, so the ball cushions and drops at your feet. Then you are ready to shoot or pass.

facts.text: His 35-yard bicycle kick for Sweden against England won the 2013 FIFA Puskás Award for the best goal of the year.
At Paris Saint-Germain he finished as Ligue 1's top scorer three times, and in his first season at Manchester United he won the EFL Cup and the Europa League.

Ferenc Puskás.why: Puskás controlled the ball mostly with his left foot, and he could shoot powerfully from far out, even from 30 metres or more. He also took direct free kicks and passed and crossed quickly and precisely. He was clever too, changing positions quickly so defenders could not keep track of him. He got his nickname, 'the Galloping Major', because his club team was run by the army. Kids can copy his love of practising with one magic foot.

learn.text: Practise a first touch that sets up your shot. As the ball arrives, use the sole or inside of your stronger foot to move it half a step to the side. Now it sits in the perfect spot, and you can strike before the defender closes in.

facts.text: Puskás became an Olympic champion in 1952, when Hungary beat Yugoslavia 2-0 in the final in Helsinki. In 1953 he helped Hungary beat England 6-3 at Wembley.
In the 1960 European Cup final he scored four goals, as Real Madrid beat Eintracht Frankfurt of West Germany by seven goals to three.

Luis Suárez.why: Suárez was a natural scorer. His Barcelona coach, Luis Enrique, said he needed very little to finish a chance. But he was more than a goalscorer: he dribbled through defences, loved a cheeky nutmeg and set up lots of goals for team-mates. In one Spanish season he led the league in both goals and assists. Kids can copy his hunger: always be ready, because a half-chance can become a goal.

learn.text: To nutmeg a defender, wait until they open their legs to block you. Then poke the ball quickly between their feet with the inside or toe of your foot, and run around them to collect it. Keep it a surprise and only try it when their legs are wide.

facts.text: Suárez helped Uruguay win the 2011 Copa America and was named Best Player of the tournament. Earlier, he captained Ajax and was Dutch Footballer of the Year.
In 2015-16 he scored 40 La Liga goals to win the Pichichi Trophy, and he became the first player to lead the league in both goals and assists.

Zico.why: Zico is remembered as one of the greatest free-kick takers of all time. He also had excellent vision and was a brilliant passer and an excellent finisher. He was naturally right-footed, but he practised so much that he became essentially two-footed. As a playmaker he could create goals for others or score them himself. Kids can copy his dedication: keep practising your weaker foot until defenders can't tell which one you prefer.

learn.text: Pass with your weaker foot every day. Stand a few big steps from a friend and pass back and forth using only that foot. Point your toe up and lock your ankle. When it feels easy, move further apart.

facts.text: Zico was named the most valuable player of the match as Flamengo beat Liverpool 3-0 in the 1981 Intercontinental Cup in Tokyo.
His 508 goals make him Flamengo's top scorer ever. Many years later, as head coach of the Japan national team, he won the 2004 Asian Cup.

Mia Hamm.why: Hamm was a forward known for her speed, footwork and stamina. With the ball she had control, pace and elegance, and she was an agile dribbler who loved to take on defenders. She struck the ball powerfully and accurately. Just as important, she was a hard-working team player who always put the team first. Kids can copy her mix of skill and effort: be brave enough to dribble, then run hard to help when you lose it.

learn.text: Run at a defender with the ball close. Just before you reach them, change speed: slow down for a moment, then explode past them. A sudden change of pace beats defenders far more often than a fancy trick.

facts.text: Hamm made her debut for the United States at 15, and she helped the University of North Carolina win four NCAA Division I championships.
In 2001 she won the first-ever FIFA World Player of the Year award for women, and she won it again in 2002.

Megan Rapinoe.why: Rapinoe was a winger famous for precise crosses and dangerous set pieces. She could curl corners straight into the net and score direct free kicks. One of her coaches called her one of the most exciting, creative and unpredictable players in the women's game. She was never afraid to try something bold. Kids can learn from her delivery: a well-aimed cross can create a goal out of nothing.

learn.text: Before you cross, look up and pick a target area, like the penalty spot or the space in front of the goalkeeper. Strike the side of the ball with the inside of your foot so it curves away from the keeper and towards your team-mate.

facts.text: Rapinoe won Olympic gold in 2012 and was the first player, male or female, to score directly from a corner at the Olympic Games, which she did twice.
At the 2011 World Cup her cross in the 122nd minute set up Abby Wambach's equaliser against Brazil. In 2019 she won the Ballon d'Or Féminin.

Abby Wambach.why: Abby Wambach was a big, brave centre-forward who made defenders' lives hard every single game. She fought for every loose ball inside the box and never stopped chasing, even in the last seconds of a match. Team-mates trusted her to finish whatever chance came her way. She also led by example, shouting encouragement and lifting players around her. Kids can copy her refusal to give up: when a game looks lost, keep running, keep demanding the ball and keep believing.

learn.text: Wambach was brilliant at arriving in the box at just the right moment for a cross. Wait outside the area, watch the winger, then sprint in as the ball is struck. Meet it with your foot and guide it low past the keeper.

facts.text: Wambach won Olympic gold medals with the United States twice, first at Athens in 2004 and again at London in 2012.
She was named FIFA Women's World Player of the Year for 2012, becoming the second American to win it after Mia Hamm.

Birgit Prinz.why: Birgit Prinz was a tall, strong German forward who could shield the ball from almost any defender. With her back to goal she held possession, waited for team-mates to join, then laid the ball off or spun to shoot. Her shots were hard and accurate from both close range and distance. She stayed calm in finals, when nerves get to most players. Young strikers can learn from how she used her body to protect the ball and bring others into the attack.

learn.text: Prinz often received with her back to goal, kept the defender behind her, then passed back to a running team-mate. Try it yourself: get side-on, keep the ball on your far foot, play a short pass back and spin to look for the return.

facts.text: Prinz played in the 1995 World Cup final against Norway when she was only 17. She remains the youngest player ever to appear in a Women's World Cup final.
With her club 1. FFC Frankfurt, Prinz lifted the UEFA Women's Cup three times, in the 2001-02, 2005-06 and 2007-08 seasons.

Christine Sinclair.why: Christine Sinclair led Canada's attack for more than twenty years and wore the captain's armband with quiet pride. She was a complete striker: clever with her runs, tidy on the ball, and deadly when a chance fell to her. She rarely wasted a shot, choosing placement over power. Off the ball, she worked hard so younger players could shine. Kids can learn from her patience: she kept doing the simple things well, season after season, and the goals kept coming.

learn.text: Sinclair scored many goals by being the first to react after a shot. Whenever you or a team-mate shoots, don't stand and watch. Sprint towards goal straight away, because the keeper might spill it or it might bounce off the post.

facts.text: Sinclair captained Canada to Olympic bronze medals in 2012 and 2016, then to the gold medal at the Tokyo 2020 Games.
In 2012 she received the Lou Marsh Trophy as Canada's athlete of the year, the first footballer ever to win it.

Alex Morgan.why: Alex Morgan was one of the fastest forwards of her era, always looking to race into the space behind a defence. She timed her runs so she stayed onside and then burst clear before defenders could turn. Once through, she kept calm and picked her spot. She also worked hard to press defenders when her team lost the ball. Young players can copy how she watched the passer's body, ready to sprint the moment the pass was coming.

learn.text: Morgan loved sprinting into the gap behind defenders. Stand level with the last defender, watch your team-mate on the ball, and start your run just as they look up to pass. Arc your run so you stay onside, then finish early.

facts.text: At the 2012 London Olympics, Morgan scored the winner against Canada in the 123rd minute of the semi-final, and the USA went on to win gold.
In the opening group game of the 2019 World Cup in France, Morgan scored five goals against Thailand, and she went on to win the tournament's Silver Boot.

Carli Lloyd.why: Carli Lloyd was a powerful midfielder who seemed to save her best for the biggest nights. She could run all game and still have the energy to strike a shot from far out in the final minutes. Lloyd trained extremely hard on her own, working on fitness and shooting long after practice ended. She believed she could score from anywhere. Kids can take her lesson: extra practice on the basics gives you confidence when the pressure is highest.

learn.text: Lloyd was famous for shooting from distance. Take a touch out of your feet, lock your ankle with toes pointing down, and strike through the middle of the ball with your laces. Land on your kicking foot to keep the shot low.

facts.text: Lloyd scored the winning goal in two Olympic gold medal matches: the extra-time winner against Brazil in 2008 and both goals against Japan in 2012.
She was named FIFA Player of the Year in both 2015 and 2016, after also winning the Golden Ball at the 2015 World Cup.

Hope Solo.why: Hope Solo was an athletic goalkeeper with quick hands and fearless dives. She came off her line confidently to claim crosses and closed down strikers bravely in one-on-ones. Because she had once played outfield, she was comfortable with the ball at her feet too. In tense matches she stayed focused and made the big save when her team needed it. Young keepers can copy her ready stance and the way she always expected the next shot to come.

learn.text: Solo's hands were strong and safe. For shots at chest height or above, make a W shape with your thumbs nearly touching behind the ball. For low shots, scoop the ball into your arms like a basket and hug it close.

facts.text: In a friendly against South Africa on 9 July 2016, Solo became the first female goalkeeper to reach 100 shutouts in international football.
She played as a forward at Richland High School and switched to goalkeeper for good at the University of Washington.

Nadine Angerer.why: Nadine Angerer was a goalkeeper who talked constantly, guiding her defenders into the right spots before danger arrived. She read the game well, so she was often standing in the perfect place when a shot came. Her calm nature made her especially good in penalty shoot-outs and nervy finals. Her saves in finals gave team-mates the confidence to attack. Kids in goal can learn that organising your team with clear, early shouts can stop chances before they happen.

learn.text: Angerer was always in the right position. Imagine a line from the ball to the middle of your goal and stand on it. Take small steps as the ball moves, so the striker sees as little of the net as possible.

facts.text: In the 2007 World Cup final against Brazil, Angerer saved a penalty taken by Marta, the Brazilian star, and Germany went on to win the match 2-0.
Germany beat Norway 1-0 in the final of the 2013 European Championship, and Angerer saved two penalties during that match, from Trine Ronning and Solveig Gulbrandsen.

Formiga.why: Formiga was a tireless defensive midfielder who kept going for more than two decades at the top level. She won the ball back, gave it to a team-mate nearby and moved again, over and over. She was never selfish, always putting the team first. Her long career shows what happens when you look after your fitness and love the game. Kids can copy her simple style: win it, pass it, support, and help the players around you.

learn.text: Formiga worked like part of a team of ants. When a team-mate presses the attacker, don't rush in too. Stand a few steps behind them at an angle, ready to win the ball if the dribbler gets past.

facts.text: Formiga is the only player to appear in seven Olympic women's football tournaments, from the first in 1996 through to 2020.
Her nickname means 'ant' in Portuguese. She earned it as a teenager because her unselfish play reminded others of ants working together.

Homare Sawa.why: Homare Sawa was a midfielder with superb vision who also knew exactly when to sneak forward. She would pass, keep moving and appear unmarked in the box just as the ball arrived. As captain she stayed calm and encouraged her team-mates, even in the toughest moments. Her career at the top lasted more than twenty years. Kids can learn from her timing: after you pass, don't stop, because the best chance often comes from the run you make next.

learn.text: Sawa loved to pass and then run into space for the return. Play a firm pass to a team-mate, then sprint past the defender straight away. Your partner taps it back into your path, and you are through on goal.

facts.text: Sawa made her debut for Japan at just 15 and scored four goals in that very first match, a win against the Philippines.
She was named FIFA Women's World Player of the Year for 2011, the first Asian player to receive the award.

Sun Wen.why: Sun Wen was a quick-thinking Chinese forward who found space where there seemed to be none. She drifted between defenders, checked away from them and then darted into the gap. Her technique let her finish neatly with either foot, and she was dangerous from set pieces. She helped turn China into one of the strongest teams of the 1990s. Young players can copy how she kept moving to lose her marker before the pass was even played.

learn.text: Sun Wen was clever at getting free. Take two steps away from the defender, then cut back towards the ball. Open your body as it arrives so you can turn and face goal in one smooth touch.

facts.text: Sun Wen led China to a silver medal in women's football at the 1996 Summer Olympics in Atlanta, the first Games to include a women's tournament.
She helped China win the Asian Cup four times in a row, in 1991, 1993, 1995 and 1997, and also won Asian Games gold in 1994 and 1998.

Michelle Akers.why: Michelle Akers was a powerful attacking star who later moved back into midfield and became the engine of her team. She struck the ball with huge force and was very hard to knock off the ball. She played through pain and tiredness, never letting her team down. Akers helped make women's football popular in the United States when it was still new. Kids can learn from her toughness and from how she changed position to help her team win.

learn.text: Akers hit the ball with real power. Put your standing foot beside the ball, pointing at the target. Keep your head down and still, then swing your kicking leg through and strike with your laces.

facts.text: Akers scored the first goal in the history of the US women's national team, in a 2-2 draw with Denmark in 1985.
In 2004 she and Mia Hamm were the only two women named in the FIFA 100, a list of great players chosen by Pele.

Kristine Lilly.why: Kristine Lilly was a hard-working wide player who seemed to have endless energy. She raced up the wing to deliver crosses, then sprinted back to help her defenders. Coaches loved her because she did the unglamorous jobs as well as the exciting ones. She stayed at the top for over two decades by looking after her fitness. Young wingers can copy her habit of tracking back, which makes a team much harder to beat.

learn.text: Lilly always ran back when her team lost the ball. As soon as possession is lost, sprint towards your own goal and get between the attacker and the net. Then turn, slow down and face the ball.

facts.text: Lilly made her debut for the United States national team in 1987, while she was still a student at high school, years before the first Women's World Cup.
She won Olympic gold in 1996 and 2004 and silver in 2000, and she played at five World Cups from 1991 to 2007.

Lieke Martens.why: Lieke Martens was a skilful Dutch winger who loved taking on defenders. She ran at them with the ball close to her feet, used quick feints, then cut inside to shoot or cross. She could use both feet, which made her hard to predict. Her confidence on the ball lifted her team in big tournaments. Kids can learn from her bravery: when you have space in front of you, attack it and make the defender decide.

learn.text: Martens would dip her shoulder one way and go the other. Dribble at the defender, lean as if you are going left, then push the ball right with the outside of your foot and speed away.

facts.text: At the 2015 World Cup in Canada, Martens scored the Netherlands' first-ever Women's World Cup goal, and it was the winner against New Zealand.
In 2021 she was part of the Barcelona side that won the Champions League, the Spanish league and the Copa de la Reina in one season.

Roberto Baggio.why: Roberto Baggio was an elegant forward who could dribble past players as if they were standing still. He played just behind the striker, gliding with the ball and spotting chances others missed. His free kicks and calm finishes made him a fan favourite all over Italy. Baggio played with joy and imagination, often trying something unexpected. Young players can copy his soft touch, keeping the ball close so they can change direction in a flash.

learn.text: Baggio's ball never got far from his feet. Dribble slowly using small touches with the inside and outside of each foot. Keep the ball close enough to change direction at any moment, then speed up.

facts.text: Baggio is the only Italian player to have scored at three different World Cups, and his goal against Czechoslovakia in 1990 was called the goal of the tournament.
He helped Juventus win the 1993 UEFA Cup, beating Borussia Dortmund 6-1 on aggregate in the final. It was the only European club trophy of his career.

Francesco Totti.why: Francesco Totti was a creative forward who could see passes long before anyone else. He often dropped deep to collect the ball, then sent a team-mate through on goal. He was also famous for cheeky chipped finishes over goalkeepers. Totti became a symbol of his home city of Rome because of his loyalty. Kids can learn from his awareness: he always knew where his team-mates were before the ball reached him.

learn.text: Totti knew his next pass before the ball arrived. As a pass comes towards you, take a quick look over each shoulder. Spot where team-mates and opponents are, so you can play forward on your first or second touch.

facts.text: Totti made his senior debut for Roma at 16 in a Serie A match in March 1993, and he later won the league title with them in 2000-01.
Totti won the European Golden Shoe in 2007, the prize for Europe's top league scorer, after finishing the 2006-07 season as Serie A's leading goalscorer.

Alessandro Del Piero.why: Alessandro Del Piero was a graceful forward with wonderful technique and a famous curling shot. He liked to drift in from the left, open up his body and bend the ball into the far corner. He was also a master of free kicks. As captain he stayed loyal to his club through good times and hard times. Young players can learn his habit of shaping the body early, so a curled finish becomes natural.

learn.text: Del Piero set up his curling shots with his first touch. Let the ball roll across you and touch it with your back foot into space. Now your body is open, ready to curl it with the inside of your foot.

facts.text: Del Piero holds the Juventus club records for both most goals and most appearances, with 290 goals in 705 games for the Turin club.
In the 2007-08 season Del Piero finished as Serie A's top scorer for the very first time, with 21 goals, just one more than his team-mate David Trezeguet.

Dennis Bergkamp.why: Dennis Bergkamp was a deep-lying forward whose touch on the ball looked like magic. He could kill a fast pass dead or flick it into space with one touch, leaving defenders turned around. He loved making goals for others as much as scoring them. He played calmly, always thinking one move ahead. Kids can learn from his first touch: he decided where the ball should go before it arrived, so his first contact set up his next action.

learn.text: Bergkamp's first touch always moved the ball somewhere useful. Before the pass arrives, pick a space to move into. Use a soft touch with the inside of your foot to push the ball there, away from the nearest defender.

facts.text: At the 1998 World Cup he scored a memorable winning goal in the final minute of the Netherlands' quarter-final against Argentina.
In February 2014, Arsenal unveiled a statue of Bergkamp outside the Emirates Stadium. He won three Premier League titles with the club.

Raúl.why: Raúl was a smart Spanish striker who did not rely on speed or size. Instead he read the game brilliantly, finding the right spot in the box before defenders noticed. In front of goal he stayed cool, often lifting the ball gently over the goalkeeper. He also worked hard for his team and led by example as captain. Young strikers can copy his calm finishing: look up, see where the keeper is, and place the ball rather than blast it.

learn.text: Raúl stayed calm when he was through on goal. Instead of hitting it as hard as you can, look at the goalkeeper. If they come out, slide it past them low or gently lift it over them.

facts.text: Raúl was the first player to score in two Champions League finals, against Valencia in 2000 and Bayer Leverkusen in 2002.
His 44 goals made him Spain's record scorer until David Villa equalled him in 2010 and passed him in March 2011.

Andriy Shevchenko.why: Andriy Shevchenko was a fast, direct striker who could shoot powerfully with either foot. He loved running at the defence, getting half a yard of space, then hitting the target before the keeper was set. Because he used both feet, defenders could never show him one way. He scored goals in Ukraine, Italy and England. Kids can learn from his practice of using both feet, which makes any attacker twice as dangerous.

learn.text: Shevchenko could score with his right or his left. Spend part of every practice shooting with your weaker foot. Start close to goal, aim for the corners, and move further back once you feel confident.

facts.text: Shevchenko is the all-time top scorer for Ukraine's national team, with 48 goals, and he was twice the top scorer in Serie A with AC Milan.
As captain, he led Ukraine to the quarter-finals of the 2006 World Cup in Germany, which was the country's first-ever appearance at the tournament.

Paolo Rossi.why: Paolo Rossi was a slim, quick striker who lived in the penalty area. He wasn't the strongest player, but his reactions were lightning fast. He seemed to know where a rebound or loose ball would drop and got there first. His sharp movement let him lose defenders for a split second, which was all he needed. Young players can copy his alertness: always expect the ball to come to you in the box, and be ready to pounce.

learn.text: Rossi was a master at reacting first. When the ball is near goal, stay on your toes, not your heels. If a shot is blocked or saved, move instantly towards the loose ball and tap it in.

facts.text: Besides the Golden Boot, Rossi won the Golden Ball as the best player of the 1982 World Cup, and he opened the scoring in the final against West Germany.
With Juventus, Rossi won Serie A in 1981-82 and 1983-84, and then the European Cup in 1985, in his final season at the club.

George Weah.why: George Weah was an explosive forward who combined speed, strength and close control. He could pick the ball up deep in his own half and carry it past several players before shooting. His power made him hard to stop, while his skill let him beat defenders in tight spaces. Weah inspired a generation of African footballers. Kids can learn from his confidence when running with the ball into open space.

learn.text: Weah loved long runs with the ball. When there's space ahead, push the ball a few steps in front and sprint after it. When a defender gets close, take smaller touches to keep it safe.

facts.text: In 1995, Weah won FIFA World Player of the Year and the Ballon d'Or, completing a rare double of the two biggest individual awards in world football.
He won the Coupe de France with Monaco in 1991 and later won Serie A twice with AC Milan, in 1996 and 1999.

Kenny Dalglish.why: Kenny Dalglish was a clever Scottish forward who was brilliant at protecting the ball. He would back into a defender, keep them away with his body, then turn or lay the ball off. He scored many goals himself, but he also created plenty for team-mates. His intelligence on the pitch made him a hero at Celtic and Liverpool. Young players can copy how he used his body as a shield to keep possession under pressure.

learn.text: Dalglish kept the ball by putting his body between it and the defender. Stand side-on, arms out for balance, and keep the ball on the foot furthest from your opponent. Roll it with your sole to stay out of reach.

facts.text: Dalglish scored the winning goal in the 1978 European Cup final against Club Brugge, in his first season at Liverpool.
He earned 102 caps for Scotland, a joint national record, and scored more than 100 league goals in both Scotland and England.

Michael Laudrup.why: Michael Laudrup was a smooth Danish playmaker who made passing look easy. He glided past opponents with the ball and then slipped passes into gaps nobody else saw. Often he would look one way and pass the other, fooling whole defences. He played with style and grace at some of Europe's biggest clubs. Kids can learn from his habit of keeping his head up, so he always knew where his team-mates were running.

learn.text: Laudrup often looked one way and passed the other. When you have the ball, glance at one team-mate to draw the defender's attention. Then play your pass to a different team-mate who is free.

facts.text: Laudrup won five La Liga titles in a row: four with Barcelona from 1991 to 1994, then a fifth with Real Madrid.
In November 2006, the Danish Football Union named Laudrup the best Danish footballer of all time. He also won the 1995 Confederations Cup with Denmark.

Gheorghe Hagi.why: Gheorghe Hagi was a creative Romanian playmaker with a magical left foot. He could dribble past defenders, spot a pass through a crowd or try a shot from almost anywhere. He took responsibility in big games and loved having the ball. His vision and imagination made Romania exciting to watch in the 1990s. Young players can learn from how he practised with his favourite foot until it could do almost anything.

learn.text: Hagi used his left foot like a paintbrush. Dribble around the area using only the inside and outside of your stronger foot. Try to change direction sharply through small gaps without the ball escaping.

facts.text: Hagi shares the record of Romania's all-time top goalscorer with Adrian Mutu, with 35 goals each, and he won four Turkish league titles with Galatasaray.
He captained Galatasaray to the 1999-2000 UEFA Cup and then helped them win the 2000 UEFA Super Cup against Real Madrid.

Rui Costa.why: Rui Costa was a graceful Portuguese playmaker who controlled games from the middle of the pitch. He kept the ball close, glided away from pressure and then released perfectly weighted passes for his forwards. He rarely rushed, choosing the right moment to play. Many fans in Florence and Lisbon remember him as a true artist with the ball. Kids can learn from the care he put into every pass, making it easy for team-mates to control.

learn.text: Rui Costa's passes always arrived at the right speed. Pass with the inside of your foot, ankle firm, and follow through towards your partner. Aim for their front foot so they can take it in their stride.

facts.text: As a youngster, Rui Costa scored the winning penalty in the 1991 FIFA World Youth Championship final, after Portugal drew 0-0 with Brazil.
He won the Coppa Italia twice with Fiorentina, in 1996 and 2001, and later won Serie A with Milan in 2003-04.

Clarence Seedorf.why: Clarence Seedorf was a strong, skilful midfielder who could do a bit of everything. He protected the ball with his body, carried it forward through midfield and hit fierce shots from distance. He was comfortable in several midfield roles and adapted to different coaches and teams. His long career at the very top came from hard work and a love of learning. Young players can copy how he stayed calm and strong when opponents pressed him.

learn.text: Seedorf was very hard to knock off the ball. When a defender comes close, lower your body, keep the ball on your far side and use your arm for balance. Then pass to a free team-mate once you have space.

facts.text: Seedorf won the Champions League four times: with Ajax in 1995, Real Madrid in 1998, and AC Milan in 2003 and 2007.
He made his Ajax debut in November 1992 at 16, the youngest debutant in the club's history at that time.

Claude Makélélé.why: Claude Makélélé was a defensive midfielder who rarely made headlines but made his team far stronger. He sat in front of the defence, read where the danger was coming from and stepped in to win the ball. Then he passed it simply to a more attacking team-mate. His quiet, clever work freed others to attack. Kids can learn that the simple jobs, done well every time, are just as valuable as scoring goals.

learn.text: Makélélé kept things simple after winning the ball. As soon as it is yours, look for the nearest free team-mate and pass it quickly and accurately. Then move to a new space so they can pass back.

facts.text: Makélélé won the French championship with Nantes in 1995 and La Liga twice with Real Madrid, in 2000-01 and 2002-03.
At Chelsea, Makélélé won the Premier League in back-to-back seasons, 2004-05 and 2005-06, after earlier lifting the 2002 Champions League with Real Madrid.

Michael Owen.why: Michael Owen burst onto the scene as a teenager with blistering speed. He loved running straight at defenders, forcing them to back off, then darting past before they could react. Once clear, he finished quickly and cleanly. He made scoring look simple because he arrived at the ball before anyone else. Young players can copy his sudden changes of pace: a slow dribble that turns into an explosive sprint is very hard to defend.

learn.text: Owen would jog with the ball, then explode. Dribble slowly towards a defender to make them relax. Then push the ball past them into space and sprint after it as fast as you can.

facts.text: Owen scored both of Liverpool's goals, late in the game, as they came from behind to beat Arsenal 2-1 in the 2001 FA Cup final.
In 1998 Owen was named PFA Young Player of the Year. That same season he shared the Premier League Golden Boot after scoring 18 league goals for Liverpool.

Gary Lineker.why: Gary Lineker was a sharp penalty-box striker who scored lots of goals from close range. He was quick over short distances and always found a yard of space in front of his marker. He rarely needed more than one touch to finish. He was also famous for playing fairly and respecting opponents and referees. Kids can learn from his clever runs to the near post and from his sportsmanship, which earned respect everywhere he played.

learn.text: Lineker scored many goals by getting in front of his defender. When a team-mate is about to cross, take a quick step away from your marker, then dart in front of them towards the near post and steer it in.

facts.text: Lineker is the only player to have been the top goalscorer in England's top division with three different clubs: Leicester City, Everton and Tottenham.
In his first season at Barcelona, Lineker scored a hat-trick in a 3-2 win over Real Madrid, and in 1989 he won the European Cup Winners' Cup with the club.

Ivan Rakitić.why: Ivan Rakitić was a tireless Croatian midfielder who covered the pitch from one box to the other. He kept the ball moving with neat, accurate passes and helped his defenders when needed. When he saw space, he struck powerful shots from outside the area. He was also cool under pressure, ready to take responsibility in tense moments. Young players can copy his work rate and the way he always offered a passing option.

learn.text: Rakitić always made himself available. After you pass, move straight away into a space where your team-mate can see you. Make a triangle shape with the ball and another player so there is always an easy pass.

facts.text: Rakitić captained Sevilla to the 2013-14 Europa League and was man of the match in the final. He won the competition again with Sevilla in 2023.
At the 2018 World Cup in Russia, Rakitić scored the deciding kick in Croatia's penalty shoot-outs against both Denmark and the hosts, Russia.

Raphaël Varane.why: Raphaël Varane was a quick, composed centre-back who rarely looked rushed. His recovery pace let him catch attackers who seemed to have escaped. He read the game early, stepping in to intercept passes before trouble started. Even in big finals he stayed calm and made smart decisions. Kids can learn from his patience in one-on-ones: instead of diving in, he stayed on his feet and waited for the right moment to win the ball.

learn.text: Varane stayed on his feet when defending. Get close to the attacker, stand side-on with knees bent, and shuffle backwards with them. Only reach in for the ball when they take a heavy touch.

facts.text: Varane joined Real Madrid from Lens in 2011 and won La Liga with them three times, in 2011-12, 2016-17 and 2019-20.
Varane was part of the France squad that won the UEFA Nations League in 2021, and in 2024 he lifted the FA Cup with Manchester United.

Juan Román Riquelme.why: Juan Román Riquelme was a classic Argentine number ten who seemed to play at his own speed. While others rushed, he paused on the ball, drew defenders towards him and then slipped a pass into the space they had left. He protected the ball superbly and was dangerous from free kicks. Fans at Boca Juniors adored him. Young players can learn that slowing down for a moment can create the perfect passing chance.

learn.text: Riquelme often stopped the ball and waited. Put your sole on the ball, keep your head up and let a defender come to you. As they step in, pass to the team-mate they just left free.

facts.text: Riquelme helped Boca Juniors win the 2000 Intercontinental Cup, beating Real Madrid in Tokyo, and he was named South American Footballer of the Year in 2001.
Riquelme captained Argentina to victory at the 1997 FIFA World Youth Championship in Malaysia, scoring four goals during the tournament.

Jay-Jay Okocha.why: Okocha played football like a street performer. He could roll the ball under his studs, flick it over a defender's head and dance away before anyone knew what had happened. As a playmaker he wanted the ball all the time, and crowds in Germany, France and England loved watching his tricks. Copy his courage: he was never scared to try something new, and he practised with the ball every single day.

learn.text: Okocha's stepover is a fake. Swing your foot round the front of the ball without touching it, drop your shoulder that way, then push the ball off in the other direction with the outside of your other foot. Start slowly, then speed up.

facts.text: At the 2004 Africa Cup of Nations, Okocha was named the best player of the tournament. The BBC also voted him African Footballer of the Year in both 2003 and 2004.
Okocha was part of the Nigeria side that won Olympic gold at the 1996 Atlanta Games, and two years earlier he was in the squad that won the 1994 Africa Cup of Nations.

Pepe.why: Pepe was the kind of centre-back strikers hated to play against. He stayed tight, used his quick feet to stick a leg in at the last moment, and chased back even when a run looked lost. He was also fast for a big defender, so he could cover for teammates. What made him special was how long he kept going: he was still playing big tournament games for Portugal in his forties, and he loved to compete.

learn.text: Pepe never dived in. Get close to the attacker, turn your body sideways so you can run either way, and bend your knees. Stay on your toes and wait. When the ball rolls too far from their foot, that is your moment to poke it away.

facts.text: At the 2022 World Cup, Pepe scored in Portugal's 6-1 win over Switzerland. Aged 39, he became the oldest player ever to score in a World Cup knockout match.
When he started Portugal's first game at Euro 2024, Pepe was 41 years old. That made him the oldest player ever to appear at a European Championship.

Park Ji-sung.why: Park was the teammate every coach dreams of. He covered every blade of grass, closing down defenders, tracking back and then sprinting forward again. Sir Alex Ferguson often picked him for the biggest games because he could follow a star player all match and still make clever runs into space. He was not the flashiest player, but he showed that hard work, smart movement and team spirit can take you to the very top.

learn.text: Park never stood still after a pass. As soon as the ball leaves your foot, move to a new space where your teammate can see you and pass back. Keep asking yourself, "Where can I be useful now?" and jog there before the ball arrives.

facts.text: Park scored at the 2002, 2006 and 2010 World Cups, becoming the first Asian player to score at three World Cups in a row. His 2002 goal beat Portugal 1-0.
In 2009 Park started for Manchester United against Barcelona in Rome. He became the first Asian player ever to appear in a Champions League final.

Gareth Bale.why: Bale started out as a left-back, then grew into one of the most dangerous wingers in the world. His secret weapon was pace: he would knock the ball past a defender and simply outrun them. Add a thumping left foot and a love of big moments, and he became Wales' hero. Kids can learn from how he changed position and kept improving, turning his speed and shooting into match-winning weapons.

learn.text: Bale loved to knock the ball into space and race after it. When there is room in front of you, push the ball a few steps ahead with your laces, sprint onto it, then look up and shoot before the defender catches you.

facts.text: Bale made his Southampton debut aged just 16, playing as a left-back. He later won the PFA Players' Player of the Year award twice, in 2011 and 2013, with Tottenham.
Bale scored the late winner for Real Madrid in the 2014 Copa del Rey final against Barcelona, after sprinting past defender Marc Bartra from the halfway line.

Ángel Di María.why: Di María was a skinny winger with a magic left foot and huge energy. He could dribble at full speed, whip in curling crosses and pop up with goals in finals. Coaches loved that he also worked hard without the ball. His career shows that big moments suit players who stay brave: in final after final he kept asking for the ball and trying the clever pass or chip.

learn.text: Di María bends crosses away from the goalkeeper. Run to the side of the box, look up to spot your teammate, then strike across the ball with the inside of your foot so it curls into the space between the keeper and the defenders.

facts.text: Di María scored the only goal of the 2008 Olympic final against Nigeria, chipping the goalkeeper from the edge of the box to win gold for Argentina.
UEFA named Di María man of the match in the 2014 Champions League final, when Real Madrid beat Atletico Madrid 4-1 after extra time in Lisbon.

Mesut Özil.why: Özil made football look calm. He drifted into gaps between the lines, took the ball with a soft first touch and slid passes that seemed impossible. Teammates said he always knew where everyone was before the ball even reached him. He was not the fastest or strongest player, but his vision and touch made him one of the best creators of his time. His game shows how thinking ahead can beat speed.

learn.text: Özil looked around before every pass arrived. While the ball is rolling to you, turn your head quickly over each shoulder to see where teammates and opponents are. Then you already know your next pass before you even touch the ball.

facts.text: Özil was the top assist provider at the 2010 World Cup in South Africa, where a young Germany side finished third.
In the 2015-16 season Özil set up 19 Premier League goals for Arsenal. He also won three FA Cups with the club and a La Liga title with Real Madrid.

Jordi Alba.why: Alba was a small left-back who played like a winger. He would sprint up the touchline, arrive at the edge of the box at just the right moment, and either shoot or slide a pass back across goal. He and Lionel Messi built a famous understanding, with Messi lifting balls over the defence for Alba to run onto. His story proves that size does not matter if you are quick, clever and keep working.

learn.text: Alba's trick was the overlap. When your teammate has the ball out wide, sprint round the outside of them into the space ahead. Shout so they know you are coming. If they pass to you, take one touch and cut the ball back into the box.

facts.text: Barcelona's academy let Alba go in 2005 for being too small, so he moved to nearby Cornellà. He later returned to Barcelona and spent more than ten seasons there.
Alba captained the Spain team that won the 2022-23 UEFA Nations League. He was also named in the Team of the Tournament at Euro 2012.

Javier Mascherano.why: Mascherano was a defensive midfielder who also became a top centre-back at Barcelona. He managed it through clever timing, reading the game and fierce focus. He talked to teammates constantly and seemed to arrive just before danger did. Kids can learn from his attitude: he was happy to do the hard jobs nobody notices so that the attackers could shine.

learn.text: When an attacker got past him, Mascherano did not give up. Turn and sprint back towards your own goal, getting between the attacker and the goal again. Only try the tackle once you are level and the ball is on your side.

facts.text: Mascherano played for Liverpool in the 2007 Champions League final in Athens against AC Milan. He later won five La Liga titles with Barcelona.
Mascherano retired from international football with 147 caps for Argentina. At that time it made him the most-capped player in his country's history.

Carlos Tevez.why: Tevez was short, strong and full of fight. He kept the ball low and close, using his body to hold off much bigger defenders, and he chased every lost cause. He grew up in a tough neighbourhood in Buenos Aires, known as Fuerte Apache, which gave him his nickname, "El Apache". Fans everywhere loved him because he never stopped running, and his energy lifted the whole team.

learn.text: Tevez protected the ball like a wall. Keep the ball on the foot furthest from the defender, bend your knees, and put your arm and body between them and the ball. Stay low and strong, then turn away when you feel space.

facts.text: Tevez won Olympic gold with Argentina at Athens 2004 and finished as the tournament's top scorer, with eight goals in six matches.
In 2003 Tevez helped Boca Juniors win the Copa Libertadores, scoring in the final against Santos, and he was voted the best player of the tournament.

Sergio Agüero.why: Agüero was a small, powerful striker with lightning reactions inside the penalty area. He could receive with his back to goal, spin in a flash and shoot before defenders could block. He was famous for scoring all kinds of goals: tap-ins, curlers, and shots from tight angles. His nickname is "Kun". Kids can copy his sharp movement, always shuffling to find half a yard of space.

learn.text: Agüero turned in tight spaces. Before the pass arrives, peek over your shoulder. If no defender is close, open your body and let the ball roll across you, then take your first touch towards goal so you are facing it straight away.

facts.text: Agüero made his debut for Independiente aged 15 years and 35 days, the youngest ever in Argentina's top division. He beat a record held by Diego Maradona.
Agüero scored 12 Premier League hat-tricks for Manchester City, the most by any player. He broke Alan Shearer's record against Aston Villa in January 2020.

Mario Balotelli.why: Balotelli was a big, strong striker with a powerful shot. He could hold the ball up with defenders leaning on him, then turn and strike from distance. He was also known for staying incredibly cool from the penalty spot, taking his time and rolling the ball past keepers. At his best he was a match-winner, and he showed that strength and calm can work together.

learn.text: Balotelli held the ball up for teammates. When a pass comes to you with a defender behind, keep your body between them and the ball. Then play a simple pass back to a teammate running forward, and spin away for the return.

facts.text: In December 2010 Balotelli won the Golden Boy award, given to the best young player in Europe. Earlier that year he had won the treble with Inter Milan.
Balotelli was named man of the match in the 2011 FA Cup final, when Manchester City beat Stoke City 1-0. He was later picked in the Euro 2012 Team of the Tournament.

Vincent Kompany.why: Kompany was a natural leader. He organised the defence with his voice, stepped in front of strikers to win the ball, and was calm enough to start attacks with a pass. Teammates trusted him in the hardest games because he never seemed to panic. After playing, he became a coach, still teaching the same ideas about courage and teamwork. Kids can learn that a good defender talks all the time.

learn.text: Kompany always talked to his partner. When your teammate goes to press the attacker, you drop a few steps behind them at an angle, ready to help. Shout "I've got you!" so they know you are covering if they get beaten.

facts.text: Kompany was named Premier League Player of the Season for 2011-12, the year Manchester City won their first Premier League title.
Kompany began his career at Anderlecht at 17 and won the Belgian Golden Shoe in 2004. As a manager, he led Burnley to the 2022-23 Championship title in his first season.

Leonardo Bonucci.why: Bonucci was a centre-back who could pass like a midfielder. From deep in his own half he would spot a forward running and ping a long ball right onto their foot. He also read the game well, stepping across to block shots and cut out passes. For kids, he is a great example that defenders can be playmakers too: win the ball, then look forward first.

learn.text: Bonucci looked forward first when he got the ball. Before it reaches you, check where your forwards are. If a teammate is free further up, pass to them. If not, play a short, safe pass to keep the ball and try again.

facts.text: With Andrea Barzagli and Giorgio Chiellini, Bonucci formed a famous Juventus back three. Fans called it the "BBC" defence, after the players' initials.
Bonucci started for Juventus in two Champions League finals, in 2015 and 2017. He also won the Coppa Italia four times with the club.

Cesc Fàbregas.why: Fàbregas learned his football at Barcelona's famous academy and moved to Arsenal as a teenager. He was a midfield brain: he saw passes early and could thread the ball between defenders for runners. He also liked to sneak into the box late and score. Kids can learn from how young he was trusted: he understood the game so well that age did not matter.

learn.text: Fàbregas passed into space, not to feet. Watch your teammate's run, then aim the ball a few steps in front of them so they can run onto it without slowing down. Use the inside of your foot and keep the pass along the ground.

facts.text: Fàbregas became Arsenal's youngest ever first-team player in October 2003, aged 16 years and 177 days, in a League Cup game against Rotherham.
Fàbregas won the PFA Young Player of the Year award in 2008. In 2011 he scored in the Club World Cup final as Barcelona beat Santos 4-0.

Edinson Cavani.why: Cavani was a striker who defended from the front. He chased centre-backs and goalkeepers, forcing mistakes, and then sprinted back to help his team. In the box he was deadly, often finishing first time before the keeper could set. His nickname, "El Matador", means "the bullfighter". He showed kids that a striker's work starts the moment the team loses the ball.

learn.text: Cavani never assumed a shot was finished. Every time you or a teammate shoots, sprint towards the goal straight away. If the keeper drops it or it hits the post, you will be first to the loose ball for an easy finish.

facts.text: Cavani was Serie A's top scorer in 2012-13, with 29 league goals for Napoli. A year earlier he scored a penalty as Napoli beat Juventus to win the Coppa Italia.
Cavani scored 35 league goals for Paris Saint-Germain in 2016-17 and was named Ligue 1 Player of the Year for that season.

Eric Cantona.why: Cantona was a forward who liked to drop deep and link the play. He held the ball, looked up and found teammates with clever passes, then arrived to finish moves himself. His confidence spread through the young Manchester United team around him. He could chip a goalkeeper, volley from the edge of the box or slip a pass round the corner. Kids can copy his calm: head up, chest out, and play with imagination.

learn.text: Cantona loved a quick one-two. Pass to a teammate, then run straight past the defender into the space behind. Your teammate passes it back first time into your path, so the defender is left behind by two quick touches.

facts.text: Before joining Manchester United, Cantona helped Leeds United win the 1991-92 First Division, the last top-flight title before the Premier League began.
Cantona captained Manchester United in the 1996 FA Cup final and scored the only goal against Liverpool. In 2021 he was inducted into the Premier League Hall of Fame.

Thomas Müller.why: Müller was never the fastest or the most skilful player on the pitch, but he was often the smartest. His nickname, "der Raumdeuter", means "the interpreter of space", because he spotted gaps before anyone else. He would drift into the right spot, score with any part of his foot and set up teammates unselfishly. He also talked non-stop, organising those around him. Kids can learn that clever positioning can beat speed.

learn.text: Müller always hunted for empty space. When your team has the ball, look for a gap where no defender is standing and move into it. If the defenders follow you, another space opens for a teammate. Keep moving and keep looking.

facts.text: At the 2010 World Cup, aged 20, Müller won the Golden Boot as top scorer and was also named the tournament's Best Young Player.
In the 2019-20 season Müller set up 21 Bundesliga goals, breaking the league record for assists in a season. He also won two Champions Leagues with Bayern, in 2013 and 2020.

Keylor Navas.why: Navas was a goalkeeper with incredibly fast reactions. He was always balanced and ready on his toes, so he could spring sideways to tip away shots that looked certain to go in. He stayed calm under huge pressure, whether in a penalty shootout or a Champions League final. Kids can learn from his ready position and his never-give-up attitude on every shot.

learn.text: Navas was always set when the shot came. As the striker is about to kick, stop moving, feet apart, knees bent, weight on your toes and hands out in front. From that ready shape you can push off quickly in any direction.

facts.text: At the 2014 World Cup, Navas saved Theofanis Gekas' kick in the penalty shootout against Greece, sending Costa Rica into the quarter-finals.
Navas was named CONCACAF Men's Player of the Year in 2014 and again in 2017. In 2013-14, with Levante, he won La Liga's award for best goalkeeper.

Lúcio.why: Lúcio was a centre-back who loved to attack. When he won the ball, he often kept running, carrying it out of defence and past opponents to start attacks. He was also a fierce but fair tackler who read danger early. He led Brazil as captain and was trusted in the biggest matches. He showed kids that defenders can be brave on the ball too, not just in the tackle.

learn.text: Lúcio carried the ball out of defence. When you win it and there is open grass in front of you, don't just kick it away. Run forward with the ball close to your feet, head up, and pass once a defender comes to meet you.

facts.text: As Brazil captain, Lúcio scored the 84th-minute winner as Brazil came back from 2-0 down to beat the USA 3-2 in the 2009 Confederations Cup final.
Lúcio scored for Bayer Leverkusen in the 2002 Champions League final against Real Madrid. He later won three Bundesliga titles with Bayern Munich.

Ronald Koeman.why: Koeman was a defender with the shooting power of a striker. He struck the ball cleanly and hard, which made him deadly from free kicks and penalties, and his long passes could switch play in an instant. He scored far more goals than most defenders ever do. After playing, he became a coach for clubs and for the Netherlands. Kids can learn how clean striking technique turns any player into a goal threat.

learn.text: Koeman hit the ball cleanly. Place your standing foot beside the ball, pointing at the target. Lock your ankle, keep your toes down, and strike through the middle of the ball with your laces. Land on your kicking foot.

facts.text: Koeman won the 1988 European Cup with PSV Eindhoven, part of a treble season. That summer he also won Euro 1988 with the Netherlands.
As Barcelona manager, Koeman led the club to the 2021 Copa del Rey, beating Athletic Bilbao 4-0 in the final.

Ricardo Quaresma.why: Quaresma was one of football's great entertainers. He loved to use the outside of his right foot, bending passes and shots in curves that surprised keepers. He also tried rabonas, crossing one leg behind the other to kick. Defenders never knew what was coming next. His game teaches kids that every part of the foot can be useful, and that practising unusual skills can make you hard to stop.

learn.text: Quaresma used the outside of his foot all the time. Dribble slowly, pushing the ball away from you with the outside of your foot, then bring it back with the inside. Swap feet. Soon the outside will feel as natural as the inside.

facts.text: At the 2018 World Cup, Quaresma scored against Iran with a trademark trivela, curled with the outside of his foot. It was his first World Cup goal.
Quaresma scored the only goal in the 117th minute of Portugal's last-16 win over Croatia at Euro 2016. He also won the 2004 Intercontinental Cup with Porto.

Bastian Schweinsteiger.why: Schweinsteiger began as a winger and grew into a midfield general. He controlled the speed of a game, deciding when to slow things down with short passes and when to speed up with a forward ball. He also worked tirelessly to win the ball back. Teammates followed his determination. He shows kids that a midfielder's job is to keep the team ticking and never stop fighting for the ball.

learn.text: Schweinsteiger kept the ball moving. In a tight space, take one touch to control and one to pass. Move after passing so you are open again. If the opponents win it, chase straight away to win it back.

facts.text: Schweinsteiger came through Bayern Munich's youth teams and won eight Bundesliga titles with the club. He also earned 121 caps for Germany.
After the 2014 World Cup, Schweinsteiger was named Germany captain when Philipp Lahm retired. He kept the armband until his final international match in 2016.

Wesley Sneijder.why: Sneijder was a small playmaker who could pass and shoot equally well with either foot. That made him very hard to mark, because he never had a weak side. He sprayed long passes, curled free kicks and hit shots from distance. He was the key player in Inter's treble team. His story shows kids the huge benefit of practising with your weaker foot until it feels just as strong.

learn.text: Sneijder was equally good with both feet. When you pass around the triangle, use your right foot one way and your left foot the other. Keep going until your weaker foot is just as accurate. Then defenders can't push you onto one side.

facts.text: A product of the Ajax youth academy, Sneijder won the Eredivisie with Ajax in 2003-04 and La Liga with Real Madrid in his first season there, 2007-08.
At the 2010 World Cup Sneijder scored five goals, including the winner against Brazil in the quarter-final. He won the Silver Ball and the Bronze Boot.

Ruud Gullit.why: Gullit was a complete footballer: tall, quick, strong and skilful. He played as a sweeper, a midfielder and a striker, and he was good in every role. He could dribble past players, pass long and score from anywhere. Later he became a player-manager at Chelsea. His career shows kids why it is great to try different positions: each one teaches you something new about the game.

learn.text: Gullit could play anywhere. In small games, take turns being the defender, the passer and the scorer. When your team has the ball, help attack. When you lose it, help defend. Learning every job makes you a smarter teammate.

facts.text: World Soccer magazine named Gullit its Player of the Year twice, in 1987 and 1989. In 1989 he scored twice as AC Milan beat Steaua Bucharest 4-0 in the European Cup final.
As Chelsea player-manager, Gullit won the 1997 FA Cup. He became the first manager from outside the British Isles to win a major trophy in England.

Ian Rush.why: Rush was a striker who did two jobs brilliantly. Without the ball, he chased defenders and goalkeepers, so Liverpool won the ball high up the pitch. With it, he made sharp runs behind the defence and finished calmly, again and again, with either a low shot or a neat side-foot. Kids can learn from both sides of his game: hard work and clever runs win goals.

learn.text: Rush ran behind defenders at the right moment. Stand level with the last defender, watch your teammate on the ball, and start your run just as they look up to pass. Curve your run so you stay onside and get goal-side.

facts.text: Rush won the European Golden Boot in 1984 as the top league scorer in Europe. He was also voted PFA Player of the Year for the 1983-84 season.
Rush holds the record for the most goals in FA Cup finals, with five. He scored twice in 1986, twice in 1989 and once in 1992.

Peter Crouch.why: Crouch stood 2.01 metres tall, but he surprised people with how neat his feet were. He could control the ball on his chest or thigh, lay it off to teammates, and score with volleys and clever touches. He was also famous for his "robot" dance celebration. Kids can learn that whatever your size, good ball control is what makes you useful.

learn.text: Crouch was great at bringing high balls down. As the ball drops, get underneath it and relax your body. Let it land on your thigh or chest, then pull back slightly so it falls softly at your feet, ready to pass.

facts.text: On 31 March 2007, Crouch scored a perfect hat-trick for Liverpool against Arsenal: one goal with his right foot, one with his left and one with his head.
Crouch helped Liverpool win the 2006 FA Cup, setting up a Steven Gerrard goal in the final. In 2017 he scored his 100th Premier League goal, for Stoke City.

Freddie Ljungberg.why: Ljungberg was a winger who scored lots of goals for a wide player. His secret was timing: he would wait on the outside, then burst into the box at the last moment, arriving unmarked to finish. He had quick feet in tight spaces and never stopped running. He was part of Arsène Wenger's great Arsenal sides. Kids can copy how he made the late run that defenders forget to track.

learn.text: Ljungberg passed and then exploded forward. Play the ball to a teammate, then sprint into the space behind the defender before they turn. Your teammate slides it back into your path, and you arrive in the box unmarked.

facts.text: Ljungberg scored on his Arsenal debut, coming off the bench against Manchester United in September 1998. He was named Premier League Player of the Season for 2001-02.
Ljungberg made 30 league appearances in 2003-04, when Arsenal's "Invincibles" went the whole Premier League season unbeaten. He also played at the 2002 and 2006 World Cups for Sweden.

Robin van Persie.why: Van Persie had one of the sweetest left feet in football. He could volley a dropping ball, curl shots into the corner and control difficult passes with one soft touch. He also moved cleverly, drifting away from defenders to find space. He began at Feyenoord before starring in England. Kids can learn from his technique: he practised striking the ball so cleanly that hard chances looked easy.

learn.text: Van Persie's first touch set up his shot. When the ball comes to you, decide where you want it before it arrives. Cushion it gently into the space you picked, a step in front of you, so your next touch can be a shot or pass.

facts.text: In his debut season at Feyenoord, Van Persie started the 2002 UEFA Cup final, which Feyenoord won 3-2 against Borussia Dortmund.
In 2012 Van Persie won both the PFA Players' Player of the Year and the FWA Footballer of the Year awards. He then helped Manchester United win the 2012-13 Premier League.

Laurent Blanc.why: Blanc was a centre-back with the feet of a midfielder. He began his career further forward, so he was always calm with the ball, passing his way out of trouble instead of panicking. He read the game so well that he rarely needed to rush into tackles. Later he became a successful coach. Kids can learn from his composure: take a breath, look up and choose the simple pass.

learn.text: Blanc stayed calm when pressed. When a defender runs at you, don't panic and kick it away. Open your body, take a soft touch away from them and pass to the teammate who is free. Simple and calm keeps the ball.

facts.text: Blanc started at Montpellier as an attacking midfielder before moving into defence. He was named French Player of the Year in 1990 and later won the 2002-03 Premier League with Manchester United.
As a coach, Blanc led Bordeaux to the 2008-09 Ligue 1 title. He then won three Ligue 1 titles in a row with Paris Saint-Germain.

Filippo Inzaghi.why: Inzaghi was a pure goal-poacher. He was not the most skilful striker, but he lived on the shoulder of the last defender and timed his runs perfectly. He always seemed to be in the right spot for a rebound or a tap-in. Sir Alex Ferguson once joked he must have been born offside. Kids can learn how much thinking, watching and timing matter for a striker.

learn.text: Inzaghi waited on the defender's shoulder. Stand level with the last defender, not behind them. Watch the ball, not just the goal. The moment your teammate is ready to pass, sprint into the space so you arrive just as the ball does.

facts.text: Inzaghi was Serie A's top scorer in 1996-97, with 24 goals for Atalanta. He then won the league with Juventus in 1997-98.
Nicknamed "Superpippo", Inzaghi won the Champions League with AC Milan in 2003 and 2007. He also scored twice in the 2007 Club World Cup final against Boca Juniors.

Rinus Michels.why: Rinus Michels taught whole teams to think like one player. In his Total Football, a defender could pop up in attack while a forward dropped back to fill the gap, so the shape never broke. His Ajax and Netherlands sides pressed high to win the ball near the other goal. Players had to be fit, brave and clever with space. He was a strict leader who demanded hard work, and modern pressing teams still borrow his ideas.

learn.text: When a teammate runs forward from your spot, don't just stand and watch. Slide across into the gap they left behind. Then if your side loses the ball, the hole is already filled. Shout to each other, 'I've got your place!' Swapping and covering keeps the team shape strong.

facts.text: Players called Michels 'The General' because he ran his teams in a strict, demanding way and expected everyone to work hard.
At Barcelona, Michels won the Spanish league title in the 1973-74 season, with Johan Cruyff starring in his side.

Alex Ferguson.why: Alex Ferguson kept winning by building fresh teams again and again. When one great side grew old, he brought in hungry new players and young stars from the academy. His teams attacked fast down the wings and became famous for scoring late goals when a match looked lost. He asked for hard work every day and never let his players feel comfortable. That fighting spirit, playing hard until the final whistle, is his biggest lesson.

learn.text: Never stop running until the referee blows the whistle. When a teammate shoots, sprint towards the goal in case the keeper spills the ball. Ferguson's teams scored many late winners because players kept going while others stopped. Keep your legs moving right to the very end.

facts.text: Before Manchester United, Ferguson led Aberdeen to the 1983 European Cup Winners' Cup, beating Real Madrid 2-1 in the final.
In 1998-99, his Manchester United won the Premier League, the FA Cup and the Champions League, a treble no English club had won before.

Arrigo Sacchi.why: Arrigo Sacchi proved that a great coach does not need to have been a famous player. His Milan team stayed close together, with only a short gap between the front line and the back line. When the ball moved, all eleven players shifted as one block and pressed the opponent. Defenders stepped up together to catch strikers offside. He practised these movements for hours until the team moved like a well-oiled machine.

learn.text: Stay close to your teammates when you defend. If the ball goes left, everyone slides left together; if it goes right, slide right. Keep a small gap to your nearest friend so no attacker can run through. One player presses the ball while another covers just behind.

facts.text: Sacchi never played professionally and worked for years as a shoe salesman. He joked that you don't need to have been a horse to become a jockey.
In his first season at AC Milan, 1987-88, Sacchi won Serie A, the club's first league title in nine years.

Johan Cruyff (coach).why: As a coach, Johan Cruyff wanted his teams to keep the ball and attack with joy. He used a bold 3-4-3 shape with wide wingers and lots of triangles for passing. Training was full of rondos, the circle games where players pass while others chase. He believed young players from the club's own academy should grow up learning the same style, and that idea shaped Barcelona's football for years after he left.

learn.text: Play keep-ball in a small circle. Before the ball reaches you, already know where your next pass will go. Use one or two touches, then move so a friend always has an angle to find you. Calm, quick passing like this was the heart of Cruyff's teams.

facts.text: Barcelona's 1992 European Cup final was played at Wembley, and Ronald Koeman's free kick in extra time beat Sampdoria 1-0.
In his first season at Barcelona, Cruyff won the 1989 Cup Winners' Cup, beating Sampdoria 2-0 in the final in Bern.

Pep Guardiola.why: Pep Guardiola builds teams that want the ball all the time. In his positional play, players spread out into set zones so whoever has the ball always has a free teammate to find. When his team loses possession, everyone rushes to win it back within seconds. He was a deep-lying midfielder for Barcelona himself, and his teams reward clever passers who think quickly and keep the ball moving.

learn.text: When a teammate has the ball, find a spot where they can see you. Don't hide behind an opponent. Take a few steps sideways to open a clear passing line. Guardiola's players keep doing this all game, so the passer is never left without a friend to choose.

facts.text: In 2009, Guardiola's Barcelona won six trophies in one calendar year, making him the first manager in history to do so.
Manchester City finished the 2017-18 Premier League season with 100 points, the first team ever to reach that total.

Bob Paisley.why: Bob Paisley was a quiet man who let his teams do the talking. His Liverpool sides played simple pass-and-move football: give the ball, then run into a new space to get it back. He had a sharp eye for players and could tell when someone was tired or not fully fit. He served the club as a player, physio and trainer before becoming manager, and he stayed modest even while lifting the biggest trophies.

learn.text: Pass the ball to a teammate, then move straight away. Don't stand still admiring your pass. Run into an open space so your friend can play it back to you. This little pass-and-move habit was at the heart of how Paisley's Liverpool played.

facts.text: Paisley was the first manager ever to win the European Cup three times, with Liverpool in 1977, 1978 and 1981.
Before coaching, he played for Liverpool and was part of the team that won the First Division title in 1946-47.

Ernst Happel.why: Ernst Happel was a coach of few words who knew exactly what he wanted. His teams pressed high up the pitch and defended in a tight line, stepping up together to leave attackers offside. He gave each player a clear job and trusted them to do it. His sides won major trophies in several countries, which shows his simple, sharp plans worked wherever he went.

learn.text: When the other team gets the ball near their own goal, close the gap fast. Slow down as you get near, stay on your toes and bend your knees. Push the attacker towards the sideline. Happel's teams won the ball back high up the pitch like this.

facts.text: Austria's national stadium in Vienna, once called the Praterstadion, was renamed the Ernst-Happel-Stadion in his honour.
As a player, Happel defended for Rapid Vienna and helped Austria finish third at the 1954 World Cup.

Helenio Herrera.why: Helenio Herrera made Inter one of the hardest teams in the world to beat. His catenaccio system kept a spare defender, the sweeper, behind the back line to mop up any danger. When Inter won the ball, they raced forward on quick counter-attacks. He also worked on his players' minds, using short slogans to build belief. For him, fitness and motivation mattered as much as tactics.

learn.text: The moment your team wins the ball, look forward first. If there is space ahead, pass or run into it quickly before the other team can get back. A fast break with two or three players can beat a crowded defence. Herrera's Inter loved to strike like this.

facts.text: Under Herrera, Inter won Serie A three times, in 1962-63, 1964-65 and 1965-66.
Inter also became world club champions with him in charge, winning the Intercontinental Cup in both 1964 and 1965.

Vicente del Bosque.why: Vicente del Bosque was a gentle, calm coach who kept big stars happy and pulling in the same direction. His Spain team kept the ball for long spells with short, patient passes, tiring opponents out. He trusted clever midfielders and let them play. Having been a midfielder for Real Madrid, he understood the game from the middle of the pitch. His quiet manner turned dressing rooms full of famous names into one team.

learn.text: Keep the ball with short, simple passes. If there is no space forward, pass sideways or back to a friend and try again. There is no need to rush. Del Bosque's Spain often passed and passed until a gap opened, then slipped the key ball through it.

facts.text: As a midfielder, del Bosque played 441 La Liga games for Real Madrid and won five league titles with the club.
He is the only manager to have won the World Cup, the Champions League, the European Championship and the Intercontinental Cup.

Marcello Lippi.why: Marcello Lippi believed the team always comes before any single star. His sides were solid and balanced, with players who knew when to attack and when to protect the defence. He had been a sweeper himself, so he valued a calm, organised back line. He was also known for smart changes during games, bringing on substitutes who could turn a match. Everyone in his squad felt they had a real part to play.

learn.text: Balance your team. When a teammate dashes forward to attack, check that someone is still guarding your goal. If nobody is, hold back or hurry into that space. Lippi's teams kept enough players behind the ball, so one lost pass didn't turn into a goal against.

facts.text: Lippi is the first and only coach to have won both the UEFA Champions League and the AFC Champions League.
With Lippi in charge, Juventus became world club champions in 1996 by winning the Intercontinental Cup.

Giovanni Trapattoni.why: Giovanni Trapattoni was a winner for decades, in Italy, Germany, Portugal and Austria. His teams were very hard to score against. He used a mix of zonal marking and man-marking: some defenders guarded areas while others followed one opponent everywhere. Having been a defender for AC Milan, he knew exactly how to stop attackers. Lively and passionate on the touchline, he showed that hunger to win can last a whole career.

learn.text: When you mark a player, stay goal-side: between them and your own goal. Keep close enough to reach the ball, and watch both the ball and your opponent. If they run, run with them. Trapattoni's defenders made life very hard for attackers by sticking tight like this.

facts.text: As a player, Trapattoni won the European Cup twice with AC Milan, in 1963 and 1969.
His ten league titles came with Juventus (six), Inter Milan, Bayern Munich, Benfica and Red Bull Salzburg.

Bill Shankly.why: Bill Shankly arrived at a Liverpool side outside the top division and gave the whole club a fresh spark. He wanted football kept simple: pass the ball, move into space and keep it going. Training used lots of small games, so players touched the ball again and again. A fiery, funny speaker, he made fans and players believe. He and his coaches planned in the famous Boot Room, and that group produced the managers who followed him.
